The move marks a sharp reversal from Petro's presidency, when Colombia repeatedly condemned Washington's campaign of **lethal strikes on suspected drug boats** — a campaign human rights groups have criticized for killing suspects without trial.
key_points: New president **Abelardo de la Espriella** has asked Washington to extend its lethal anti-drug campaign into Colombia
Colombia becomes the **19th member** of the US-led Americas Counter-Cartel Coalition
Defense Secretary **Pete Hegseth** says Colombia authorized **joint military operations** against cartels
It's the world's **largest cocaine producer**, and the shift ends years of friction under predecessor Gustavo Petro

depth.background: Colombia is the world's largest producer of cocaine, and for decades the US has poured billions of dollars into fighting the drug trade there through aid, training and intelligence-sharing. Under outgoing president **Gustavo Petro**, ties with Washington soured badly: Petro criticized Trump's expanding military strikes on suspected drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and Pacific, which have killed dozens of people without judicial process, and Trump at one point warned Petro he would **"be next."** De la Espriella, an outsider who won the presidency campaigning on a **"wrath of God"** crackdown on traffickers, took office pledging full alignment with the US instead.

cards.title: France's tax authority confirms hackers stole taxpayer data from nearly 700,000 people
cards.what_happened: France's Finance Ministry confirmed late on **Thursday, August 14** that taxpayer data was stolen in a cyberattack. A hacker operating under the name **"ZeroBytes"** claimed on August 12 that they had broken into the DGFiP's systems using **stolen login credentials and a technique to bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA)**, and that they'd been inside since **late June**. The ministry says roughly **678,000** taxpayers' data was accessed, though the hacker claims the real number tops **2 million** records. Investigators say the unauthorized access was actually spotted and shut down in late June during routine security checks — but by then, the data had already been taken.
key_points: Hackers stole personal data belonging to around **678,000** French taxpayers, individuals and businesses
A hacker using the alias **'ZeroBytes'** claims the true haul is over **2 million** records
The intruder reportedly used **stolen credentials and an MFA bypass** to get in
The breach was quietly detected and cut off in **late June**, but only confirmed publicly this week

depth.background: France's tax authority, the **General Direction of Public Finances (DGFiP)**, holds sensitive financial data on virtually every taxpayer in the country — incomes, addresses, and bank details tied to tax filings. Government tax agencies are prime targets for cybercriminals precisely because a single breach can expose so much personal financial data at once, useful for identity theft and fraud. Attacks like this have become increasingly common against public-sector databases worldwide.

cards.title: A magnitude-7.7 earthquake off Indonesia's Flores Island kills at least 20 and triggers a tsunami warning
cards.what_happened: The quake hit at **5:58am local time on Saturday**, centered about 68km north-northwest of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province at a shallow depth of 10km. Buildings collapsed across several regencies, and residents described fleeing into the streets as the ground shook, with footage showing panicked crowds running through the port town of **Maumere**. Indonesia's geophysics agency (BMKG) issued a tsunami warning for the surrounding coastline, prompting hundreds to rush to higher ground before the warning was lifted roughly three hours later. Death-toll reports diverged through the day: East Nusa Tenggara's governor initially confirmed **5 deaths**, while a Maumere search-and-rescue official later put the toll at **20 dead**, 6 injured, and 2 still buried, with the number expected to keep changing as rescuers reach cut-off areas. Three aftershocks, up to magnitude 6.1, struck within the first half hour, and about 2,000 people evacuated in the neighboring Nagekeo regency.
key_points: A **magnitude-7.7 earthquake** struck at **5:58am local time** on Saturday, centered 68km north-northwest of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province.
Rescue teams in the port town of **Maumere** report **at least 20 dead**, six injured, and two still trapped under rubble, though the toll is still being confirmed.
Indonesia's meteorology agency issued a **tsunami warning** for nearby coastlines, which was lifted after roughly **three hours**.
**Three aftershocks** — up to **magnitude 6.1** — struck within the first half hour.
About **2,000 residents** in the neighboring Nagekeo regency evacuated to higher ground as buildings collapsed.

depth.background: Indonesia sits on the **Pacific 'Ring of Fire'**, the horseshoe-shaped belt of tectonic boundaries that produces roughly 90% of the world's earthquakes, and the archipelago has suffered several major quakes in recent years, including deadly ones on Sulawesi in 2018 and Flores itself in 2021. Flores was devastated by a **magnitude-7.8 quake and tsunami in 1992** that killed over 2,000 people, so the island's population has lived with this exact risk before. Saturday's quake struck at a shallow depth of **10km**, which tends to produce stronger surface shaking than a deeper quake of the same size. Indonesia's national disaster agency (BNPB) has deployed rescue teams, but landslide-blocked roads on the mountainous island are slowing the response.

prev_ref.title: Tankers are attacked and an oil spill spreads in the Strait of Hormuz, as Trump and Iran trade claims over who controls it

cards.title: Trump says he will soon 'declare' the Strait of Hormuz a US territory
cards.what_happened: Speaking to a crowd of law enforcement officers at the **Nassau County Police Academy** in New York on **Friday, August 14**, Trump said: 'After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated — pretty soon, I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.' He added, 'Essentially, that's what it is. We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to.' The remark came as commercial shipping through the Strait remains near a standstill, oil stockpiles are being drawn down internationally, and Iran and Oman are separately negotiating a framework to manage — and eventually reopen — the waterway without US or Israeli vessels. The US has not taken any formal legal or diplomatic step to annex or claim the strait; this was a spoken threat, not policy.
key_points: Trump told police officers at a Nassau County, New York event he'll 'pretty soon' be **declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States**.
He argued the US already runs it in practice: **'We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to.'**
The US has **no legal or historical claim** to the waterway — sovereignty over it is shared by **Iran and Oman**, not Washington.
It escalates a rhetorical fight that began days earlier when Trump claimed the US had **'total control'** of the Strait after tanker attacks and an oil spill.
Iran's government has repeatedly said the Strait remains under its **'complete management and control'**, rejecting any US claim.

thread.previously: We reported that after tanker attacks and a Russian 'shadow fleet' tanker sank and spilled oil, Trump claimed the US had 'total control' of the Strait of Hormuz and might 'keep it', while Iran insisted the waterway remained under its own 'complete management and control'.
thread.changed: Trump went a step further, saying he will soon formally 'declare' the Strait a 'territory of the United States' — an unprecedented claim with no legal basis, since the US has no sovereignty there and Oman and Iran jointly control the waterway.

depth.background: The **Strait of Hormuz** is the narrow shipping lane between Iran and Oman that roughly **a fifth of the world's oil** passes through on tankers headed from Gulf producers to global markets. Since a US-Iran conflict escalated this summer, Iran has restricted ship traffic and the US Navy has moved to enforce what it calls an **'indefinite' blockade**, while a sanctioned Russian tanker sank nearby and spilled oil. Trump has been building toward this claim for days, first saying the US had 'total control' of the waterway and now going further by threatening to formally call it American territory — something with **no basis in international law**, since the strait runs through Iranian and Omani territorial waters.

cards.title: China's tech boom isn't enough to stop its economy from slowing further
cards.what_happened: New analysis published **Friday, August 14** found China's high-tech export boom is still **failing to offset the broader slowdown** heading into the second half of 2026. The **4.3% Q2 growth figure**, confirmed in mid-July, was driven down mainly by a **historic property-investment slump (-18%)** and weak household spending, even as **semiconductor exports doubled** and EV exports rose roughly **70%** on strong overseas demand. **Retail sales rose just 1.3%** in the first half of the year, well below 2025's pace, showing Chinese consumers are still cautious. Official activity data for July, due out **Monday, August 17**, is expected to confirm the trend continued — worsened by several typhoons that disrupted shipping, factories and construction through the month. Analysts expect Beijing to lean harder on government spending (fiscal stimulus) to prop up growth, though that risks pushing China's debt levels even higher.
key_points: China's economy grew just **4.3% year-on-year in Q2 2026**, the **slowest pace since late 2022**, undershooting Beijing's own 4.5-5% target.
**Real estate investment collapsed 18%** in the first half — the biggest six-month drop on record for the sector.
**Semiconductor exports doubled** and EV shipments jumped **~70%**, showing the tech and manufacturing side is still firing.
**Retail sales grew just 1.3%** in the first half, a sharp slowdown from 3.7% growth for all of 2025 — a sign households are still not spending.
Official July activity data, due **Monday**, is expected to show further weakness, worsened by **typhoon disruption** to shipping and factories.

depth.background: China's economy has been fighting a **property-market downturn** and weak consumer spending for several years, even as its government has poured money into advanced manufacturing — semiconductors, EVs, and AI-linked hardware — to offset the slump. That split has defined 2026 so far: a **shrinking construction and property sector** dragging down growth, while **exports of high-tech goods surge**. Q2's 4.3% growth print, released in mid-July, was the weakest quarterly figure since the depths of China's COVID-era slowdown in 2022, and Israel-Iran war-driven oil price spikes added extra cost pressure on top of it.

cards.title: The US and 18 allied nations wrap up their biggest Panama Canal defense drill since 2012, amid friction over China's role
cards.what_happened: From **August 3–14, 2026**, US Southern Command led **PANAMAX 2026**, an 11-day multinational military exercise involving Panama and roughly **18 other countries**, including Brazil, Chile, Mexico and the UK. Unlike recent tabletop-only versions, this year's drills were run live and in the field — the first time that's happened since **2012**. Forces rehearsed defending the canal against simulated air and sea attacks, cyber intrusions, and narco-terrorist threats. The exercise concluded around **August 13–14** with no major incidents reported. Panama's President José Raúl Mulino insisted the canal is "not under any direct threat," pushing back on the security concerns driving the drill's scale.
key_points: The US led **PANAMAX 2026**, an 11-day war game (Aug 3–14) with **Panama and 18 other nations** rehearsing defense of the Panama Canal.
It's the first time since **2012** the exercise has run live, in the field, rather than as a tabletop simulation.
Drills covered simulated air and sea attacks, cyber-attacks, and narco-terrorist threats to the canal.
The show of force comes as **President Trump** keeps accusing China of gaining too much influence over canal operations — a claim Panama's president flatly denies.
The canal carries roughly **6% of all global maritime trade** every year.

depth.background: The **Panama Canal** is one of the world's most important shipping shortcuts, letting cargo ships skip the long, dangerous route around South America. The US built and ran the canal for most of the 20th century before handing full control to Panama in **1999** under a long-standing treaty. Since returning to office, Trump has repeatedly demanded lower tolls for US ships and accused China of quietly gaining influence over canal-adjacent ports — claims Panama's government rejects. PANAMAX exercises have run periodically for years, but 2026's was the first full live version since 2012, reflecting how seriously Washington now treats the canal's security.

cards.title: Mount Etna's eruption shuts Sicily's main airport for a sixth straight day, with ash reaching Libya
cards.what_happened: A new eruptive sequence began at Etna's Voragine crater around August 6-7, with Strombolian activity (small, frequent bursts of lava and gas) intensifying through the evening and evolving into sustained lava fountaining. Ash columns rose high enough to force repeated, rolling suspensions of all arrivals and departures at Catania airport, with authorities extending the closure day after day as the volcano kept erupting rather than settling down. By mid-week the shutdown had been extended through the early hours of Saturday, August 15, and hundreds of diverted flights were straining smaller airports in Palermo, Trapani, Comiso and Lamezia Terme. INGV scientists noted this is the volcano's second intense paroxysmal episode within a month, following one in late July, with new lateral fissures opening at lower elevations — a sign the activity is more complex than a routine paroxysm.
key_points: Europe's most active volcano has been erupting since **August 6-7**, forcing Sicily's Catania airport — Italy's **fifth-busiest** by passenger traffic — to suspend all flights for a **sixth consecutive day**.
More than **1,350 flights** have been disrupted in the past week; **36%** of nearly 2,000 scheduled arrivals between Aug 6-12 were cancelled and over **600** diverted to other airports.
The ash plume has drifted as far as Malta and **Libya**, hundreds of kilometers from the volcano, triggering aviation red alerts.
Estimated tourism-related losses for Sicily range from **€12 million to €24 million**, hitting hotels, restaurants, taxis and tour operators at the height of summer travel season.

Italy's INGV volcanology institute says this is the **second major paroxysmal sequence in under a month**, with lava fountains and new lateral fissures making the eruption's endpoint hard to predict; the closure was extended again into the early hours of August 15.

depth.background: Mount Etna, on Sicily's east coast, is Europe's tallest and most continuously active volcano, prone to short bursts called "paroxysms" — episodes of intense lava fountaining and ash emission from its summit craters. Catania's Fontanarossa airport sits directly in the volcano's shadow and has been repeatedly closed by ashfall in past eruptions, including as recently as 2024. Sicily depends heavily on this single gateway airport for its peak-season tourism economy, handling over **12 million passengers in 2025**.

cards.title: Poland says it thwarted a Russian plot to assassinate a Ukrainian-American in Warsaw
cards.what_happened: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced Thursday that the Internal Security Agency (ABW) and police arrested a Russian man on August 7 who had been recruited by Russian services to kill a Ukrainian-American — someone Tusk described as "inconvenient to the Putin regime." Tusk said authorities intervened "at the last minute" to stop what he called a planned "execution." He stressed this was carried out in cooperation with U.S. intelligence services and represents the first documented instance of Russia ordering an attack on a U.S. citizen inside another NATO member state. The suspect has been remanded into three months of pretrial detention while the investigation continues. Polish officials tied the plot to the broader pattern of Kremlin-directed sabotage and killings across Europe, including DHL parcel-bomb test runs and the November 2025 railway bombing.
key_points: Polish security services arrested a **Russian national** in Warsaw on **August 7** who had allegedly been recruited by Russian intelligence to kill a man holding both **Ukrainian and US citizenship**.
Prime Minister **Donald Tusk** called it the **first known case** of Russia ordering the killing of an American citizen on the soil of another **NATO** country.
The operation to stop the plot was run jointly with **U.S. services**, and the suspect will be held in pretrial custody for **three months**.

It follows a **June 2026** assassination of Putin critic Semyon Skrepetsky (real name Robert Kuzovkov) in eastern Poland, and a **November 2025** railway bombing Warsaw blamed on Russian intelligence.
Western officials say Moscow has run dozens of parcel-bomb, arson and sabotage plots across Europe since the **2022 invasion of Ukraine** — this is the first to target a US passport-holder directly.

depth.background: Since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, European security agencies have accused Russian military intelligence (the GRU) and the FSB of running a low-level campaign of sabotage across NATO countries — railway bombings, warehouse arson, and parcel bombs sent through courier networks like DHL. Poland, as Ukraine's key logistics and military-aid corridor and a NATO/EU border state, has been hit hardest, including a **November 2025** rail bombing and the assassination of a Russian dissident cartoonist in Poland this past **June**. Until now, these plots have targeted Ukrainian exiles, dissidents, and infrastructure — not American citizens directly.

cards.title: US consumer confidence craters to its lowest since the 2024 election, as Iran-linked inflation fears bite
cards.what_happened: The index fell to **51.0** in August from **55.2** in July, an **8% drop** that snapped two months of improvement and came in well below the **54.5** Wall Street had forecast. Survey director Joanne Hsu said sentiment fell **across the political spectrum**, with Republicans posting the steepest month-on-month decline and now sitting **19% below** where they stood just before the Iran conflict erupted — the lowest since the 2024 election. Views of people's own personal finances barely moved, but their outlook on the broader economy soured sharply: expected business conditions fell **11%** for the near term and **17%** for the long term. Year-ahead inflation expectations rose to **4.3%**, above the 3.4% reading recorded in February, before the Iran conflict began. The declines were largest among **older, lower-income, and non-college-educated consumers** — groups most exposed to any squeeze on their purchasing power.
key_points: University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index dropped to **51.0** in August, from **55.2** in July
That's an **8% monthly fall**, well below the **54.5** economists expected
Households now expect **4.3% inflation** over the next year, up from 4.2% — and above pre-Iran-conflict levels
Confidence dropped **across the political spectrum**, with Republicans seeing the steepest fall since the 2024 election
Expected business conditions sank **11% for the short term and 17% for the long term**

depth.background: The University of Michigan's monthly Surveys of Consumers is one of the most closely watched measures of how ordinary Americans feel about their finances and the economy — it doesn't measure what's actually happening, but what people *expect* to happen, which shapes real spending decisions. Sentiment had been recovering for **two straight months** before this reading. The renewed slide is tied to the **Iran conflict** that flared earlier this year, which pushed up oil prices and fed fears of a fresh round of inflation on top of an economy still digesting years of price pressure.

cards.title: A 480,000-person study finds climbing stairs cuts your risk of dying from heart disease by 39%
cards.what_happened: The pooled analysis found that people who climbed stairs often had a **39% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease** and a **24% lower risk of dying from any cause** than infrequent stair-climbers. It also found reduced rates of major cardiovascular events — **heart attack, stroke and heart failure** — among frequent stair climbers. A sub-analysis within the review found the benefit peaked around **six flights of stairs a day** (roughly 60-70 steps), suggesting even a small, consistent daily habit — not a marathon-level effort — moves the needle. The study's release was picked up by multiple outlets on **August 14**.
key_points: People who **regularly climbed stairs** were **39% less likely** to die of cardiovascular causes
They were also **24% less likely** to die from any cause, compared to those who rarely climbed stairs
The analysis pooled **nine studies covering 480,479 people**, followed for a median of **14 years**
The sweet spot was around **6 flights a day** — roughly **60-70 steps**
Stair climbing also cut rates of **heart attack, stroke, and heart failure**

depth.background: Researchers at the **University of East Anglia** and the **Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital** in the UK ran a systematic review and meta-analysis — a study that combines results from many separate studies to get a more reliable answer than any single one could give. They pulled together data from **nine high-quality studies**, covering people aged **35 to 84** (53% women), including both healthy people and those with a prior history of heart problems.

cards.title: The FIA quietly lifts its post-Ukraine-war ban on Russian and Belarusian drivers, without explaining why
cards.what_happened: The FIA's **World Motor Sport Council** — its top decision-making body — voted on **August 3, 2026** to lift the restrictions, and the decision was formally circulated to national federations, teams and officials on **August 13**. Under the new rules, Russian and Belarusian competitors, national teams and officials can take part in international events **without restriction**, and are free to display their **flags, colours and anthems** again. The requirement to sign a neutrality commitment has been scrapped. One restriction remains: **no international event can be held inside Russia or Belarus** "until further notice." The FIA gave **no public explanation** for the timing or reasoning behind the reversal, which several outlets noted was unusual given how detailed the original 2022 ban's justification had been.
key_points: FIA's World Motor Sport Council decided on **August 3** to lift restrictions, confirmed in a circular sent **August 13**
Russian and Belarusian drivers, teams and officials can now compete under their **own flags and anthems**
The mandatory **neutrality pledge** signed since 2022 no longer applies
Competitions still **cannot be held inside Russia or Belarus** itself
No public explanation was given for the reversal, four years after the war in Ukraine triggered the ban

depth.background: In March 2022, weeks after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the FIA — motorsport's global governing body — barred Russian and Belarusian competitors from racing under their national colours anywhere in the world, mirroring bans imposed by the IOC and other sports bodies. Drivers were only allowed to compete as neutral athletes, without flags, anthems or national identification, and had to sign a declaration condemning the war to be cleared to race. The measure affected everyone from junior karting racers to any Russian nationals hoping to reach Formula 1. The FIA has not previously wavered from the ban despite periodic lobbying from Russian motorsport federations.

prev_ref.title: Canada and the US race to strike a trade deal before Washington's Aug. 19 deadline for 50% tariffs

cards.title: The US offers Canada a partial tariff climbdown, but Ottawa says it doesn't go far enough to beat Friday's deadline
cards.what_happened: Canadian and US trade officials wrapped a second round of talks this week in Washington, with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer saying **President Trump and Canadian PM Mark Carney will now be given 'options'** based on where the negotiations stand. Sources on both sides say the **Americans offered a new proposal on Tuesday** that would lower some of the sectoral tariffs hitting Canadian exports — but not by enough to satisfy Ottawa's negotiators. The Americans are also pushing for a broader deal that would give the US **preferential access to Canadian critical minerals** and cover security and energy cooperation, extending well beyond the tariff dispute itself. Greer described the meetings as 'good' and 'cordial,' a notable tonal shift from earlier this month. Canada's trade minister Dominic LeBlanc and chief negotiator Janice Charette have now been in Washington on and off since Monday, racing to have a deal framework ready before Trump decides whether to greenlight the **Aug. 19 tariff deadline**.
key_points: US officials say Trump and Carney will get **'options'** to choose from after this week's Washington talks.
Washington's latest offer **lowers some sectoral tariffs — but not enough**, say Canadian negotiators.
The US is also seeking **preferential access to Canadian critical minerals** as part of any wider deal.
Talks are described as **'good' and 'cordial'**, a marked shift from an earlier blow-up over a Reagan-era ad.
The clock is still running toward the **Aug. 19 deadline** for 50% tariffs on about **$20 billion** of Canadian goods.

thread.previously: We reported Canadian and US negotiators meeting in Washington on Aug. 13, racing the Aug. 19 deadline for 50% tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian exports, with Carney calling talks 'constructive' but warning Canada 'will not accept a bad deal.'
thread.changed: The US has now put a concrete but insufficient partial-tariff-relief offer on the table, is asking for critical-minerals access as part of any wider deal, and both sides say Trump and Carney will soon be handed formal 'options' to choose from.

depth.background: Washington has threatened to hit about **$20 billion** worth of Canadian exports — including alcohol, hockey sticks and cement — with a **50% tariff** starting **Aug. 19**, and unusually, this round would carry no exemption for goods that already comply with the USMCA/CUSMA free-trade pact. The threat stems from three US grievances: Canadian provinces banning US liquor sales, Canada's retaliatory tariffs on US autos and parts, and a dairy quota system Washington says unfairly favors the EU over the US. Talks between the two sides broke down briefly earlier this month after Canada aired an anti-tariff ad using an old Reagan speech, which reportedly angered the White House. Canada has signaled it is willing to lift the liquor bans and offer concessions on autos and dairy in exchange for tariff relief.

prev_ref.title: Iran says the Strait of Hormuz is still shut despite Trump's claims, as tanker traffic sinks to a one-week low

cards.title: Ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz grinds to a near-standstill as the US threatens an 'indefinite' naval blockade
cards.what_happened: Transit through the Strait of Hormuz ground to a near-standstill on Friday after two more commercial vessels were attacked in the strait. The **United States said it could maintain its naval blockade of Iran indefinitely**, hardening a position it had earlier signaled was only temporary. A senior Iranian source said there has been **no progress** in talks meant to build on the ceasefire memorandum Presidents Trump and Pezeshkian signed in June, which had briefly restored safe passage for commercial ships. Since that ceasefire began breaking down, Iran has resumed attacking vessels it accuses of trying to transit the strait without its permission, reviving the same standoff that shut the strait for weeks earlier this summer. Shipping trackers who had clocked a partial recovery in traffic over the past week now say volumes have fallen back toward the crisis lows seen in July. Oil markets reacted to the fresh disruption risk, with crude prices firming again.
key_points: The **US now says it could keep its Hormuz naval blockade in place indefinitely**, dropping earlier hints it was temporary.
**Two more tankers were attacked** on Friday, and Iran has resumed hitting ships it says lack its permission to pass.
A senior Iranian source says **talks to revive June's ceasefire deal have made zero progress**.
Traffic through a strait that normally carries **about a fifth of the world's oil** has collapsed toward July's crisis lows.
**Oil prices rose** on the fresh disruption, feeding directly into fuel costs for import-dependent economies like India.

thread.previously: We reported Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority contradicting Trump's claim of US control, with tanker traffic down to about 8 ships a day (a one-week low) and Iran issuing a list of demands before it would fully reopen the strait.
thread.changed: Traffic has fallen further after two more tankers were attacked, the US has hardened its stance to say it could keep the blockade in place indefinitely, and an Iranian source now says the diplomatic track has made zero progress.

depth.background: The Strait of Hormuz is a roughly 33-km-wide chokepoint between Iran and Oman that ships carrying about a **fifth of global oil supply** must pass through — there is no practical alternative route for most of that cargo. Iran and the US clashed in and around the strait earlier this year after a series of tanker attacks and a US-led naval blockade; a **June memorandum of understanding**, brokered after weeks of fighting, was supposed to guarantee 60 days of free passage for commercial vessels in exchange for the US lifting its blockade. That truce has been fraying for weeks, with both sides accusing the other of violations, while a separate Russian tanker disaster has spilled oil across roughly 800 square kilometers of nearby Omani coastline, compounding the region's problems. Iran has laid out a long list of demands — including a permanent end to the blockade and compensation for war damage — before it will guarantee the strait stays open.

cards.title: OpenAI and Anthropic start cutting AI prices as cheaper Chinese models close the gap
cards.what_happened: This week, **OpenAI** substantially lowered prices on its GPT-5.6 Luna model, while **Anthropic** positioned its new Claude Opus 5 at roughly **half the price** of its top-end Fable 5 model, giving developers a materially cheaper option that still uses recent-generation technology. The moves come as China's **Z.AI** prepares to launch GLM-5.3, an upgraded model aimed squarely at coding tasks, explicitly built to close the gap with leaderboard-topping US models like Anthropic's Fable 5. Chinese competitors have been gaining developer users specifically because their pricing undercuts the US labs, forcing OpenAI and Anthropic to respond even though AI training and inference remain extremely expensive to run. The pattern mirrors last year's price cuts, but this round is happening while US AI infrastructure spending — including the $100 billion data-center IPO also making news this week — keeps climbing.
key_points: **OpenAI** substantially cut pricing on its GPT-5.6 Luna model this week.
**Anthropic** priced its Claude Opus 5 at roughly **half** the cost of its flagship Fable 5 model.
China's **Z.AI** is about to ship GLM-5.3, a coding-focused model aimed at closing the gap with US leaders.
The moves are a direct response to **lower-cost Chinese rivals** (Z.AI, DeepSeek) winning developer users.
Cheaper 'frontier' AI lowers the cost of building AI products, but squeezes the profit margins of AI labs.

depth.background: For the past few years, the most capable AI models — from **OpenAI**, **Anthropic** and **Google** — have also been the most expensive to run, priced well above cheaper, slightly-less-capable alternatives. That started to change as Chinese labs like **DeepSeek** and **Z.AI** released increasingly competitive models, often open-source or far cheaper per query, while lagging the US leaders by only months on raw capability. Because most AI products are billed by the token (unit of text processed), even a modest price gap can decide which model a company builds on, especially for high-volume uses like coding assistants.

cards.title: Israel kills a Hamas commander in Gaza's first deadly strikes in over a week, straining the fragile ceasefire
cards.what_happened: On Thursday, an Israeli strike in **Khan Younis** killed Hudhaifa Khaled Suleiman Qawari, whom the IDF described as a commander in Hamas's Khan Younis Brigade involved in training fighters, moving weapons and rebuilding the group's capabilities. Hours later, a **drone fired three missiles** at a vehicle on al-Rashid Street southwest of Gaza City, killing Colonel Jamal Abu Kamil, a 43-year-old senior official in Gaza's Hamas-run police force, and injuring two others. Gaza's health ministry said these were the **first combat deaths in more than a week**, during which Israel had scaled back strikes under US pressure while disarmament talks continued. The IDF says both men were 'advancing attacks' on Israeli troops, which it argues justifies action even inside the ceasefire. Israeli forces now hold roughly **70% of Gaza's territory**, up sharply from the ceasefire's early weeks.
key_points: The IDF killed **Hudhaifa Khaled Suleiman Qawari**, a Hamas Khan Younis Brigade commander, in a Thursday strike.
A **separate drone strike** killed a senior Gaza police official, **Colonel Jamal Abu Kamil**, and wounded two others.
These are the **first fatalities in more than a week**, breaking a rare lull under the October 2025 ceasefire.
Israeli control of Gaza territory has grown from about **53% in October to nearly 70% today**.
Hamas has formally accepted a **15-point US-backed roadmap** to disarm, but continued strikes cast doubt on it.

depth.background: A ceasefire between Israel and Hamas took effect in **October 2025**, ending the most intense phase of the Gaza war, but it was never a full peace — Israeli forces stayed inside parts of Gaza and the two sides never agreed on Hamas's disarmament. A US-backed 'Board of Peace' and an International Stabilization Force have been pushing a follow-on roadmap: Hamas gives up its weapons in phases while Israel gradually withdraws. Hamas said yes to the roadmap on paper, but on the ground Israel has kept carrying out strikes it says are pre-emptive, and its footprint inside Gaza has quietly kept expanding rather than shrinking.

prev_ref.title: US senators demand answers after sailors try to jump off the USS Abraham Lincoln during a record-length deployment

cards.title: The US Navy sends a new aircraft carrier to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln after sailors tried to jump ship
cards.what_happened: The **USS George Washington** carrier strike group, which had just finished a port visit in Vietnam on August 5, was tracked on August 14 transiting the **Strait of Malacca** — the narrow waterway between Malaysia and Indonesia that is the main shipping route from the Pacific into the Indian Ocean. US naval authorities confirmed the movement without disclosing the ship's final destination, citing operational security. A US official told reporters the carrier is headed to relieve the **USS Abraham Lincoln**, which has now been deployed for more than **250 days**, including over **200 days without making a single port call** — a punishing stretch that has fed the crew-morale concerns senators raised this week. The handoff had reportedly been planned in advance, but its timing lands right after the jump-attempt controversy became public.
key_points: The **USS Abraham Lincoln** has been deployed over **250 days** — more than **200 days without a single port call**.
The **USS George Washington** strike group is now confirmed moving through the **Strait of Malacca** toward the Middle East.
The swap follows reports of **crew morale problems**, including sailors attempting to jump overboard.
The move will leave the **Pacific without a US carrier presence** for an unknown stretch.
A US official says the swap was **'previously planned'** — not a panic reaction, but its timing follows the morale controversy.

thread.previously: US senators publicly demanded answers after multiple sailors tried to jump overboard from the USS Abraham Lincoln, which had been at sea for a record-setting stretch supporting the war on Iran.
thread.changed: The Navy has now confirmed it is actually moving to relieve the Lincoln: the USS George Washington carrier strike group, fresh off a port visit in Vietnam, has been tracked transiting the Strait of Malacca toward the Middle East to take over.

depth.background: The Lincoln was diverted from a routine deployment last November and redirected into the Middle East as the **US war with Iran**, now in its sixth month, dragged on. Extended, uninterrupted sea time is normally capped for exactly this reason: fatigue, isolation, and lack of shore leave erode a crew's mental health over months at sea. When senators demanded answers this week after sailors tried to jump from the ship, the Navy was already facing pressure to act. The Lincoln has effectively been the US Navy's forward floating base for operations tied to the Strait of Hormuz standoff.

cards.title: Treasury Secretary Bessent vows 'economic isolation' of Iran unlike anything seen before, with details due next week
cards.what_happened: Speaking to Newsmax's 'Rob Schmitt Tonight' on the evening of **August 13**, Bessent said: **'Watch this space for more announcements coming next week because we are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of the economic isolation of a country.'** He described the coming plan as **'a combination of economic isolation like the world has never seen before, and the continued blockade in the Strait of Hormuz that will keep anything from going in or out of the Iranian ports.'** He did not detail what the specific new measures would be, only that they are still being finalized. The comments confirm that Washington's strategy going forward leans on financial and trade pressure rather than a wider bombing campaign.
key_points: Bessent says the US will apply sanctions **'like have never been seen'** in the history of isolating a country.
New measures are due to be announced **'next week.'**
The plan pairs new sanctions with the **continued naval blockade** of Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz.
It signals the US is leaning on **economic pressure instead of an all-out bombing campaign** against Tehran.
Bessent has already issued a **series of sanctions** on Iranian figures and proxies over the past year.

depth.background: The US has been at war with Iran for roughly six months, largely fought through air power, a naval blockade, and sanctions rather than a ground invasion. Treasury Secretary **Scott Bessent** has been the point person for the sanctions side of that campaign, repeatedly targeting Iranian officials, front companies, and militia proxies funded by Tehran. His comments this week suggest the administration is preparing to escalate that economic track sharply, even as the military side — carrier deployments, the Hormuz blockade — continues in parallel.

cards.title: Israeli settlers besiege Palestinian homes in the West Bank for five nights, drawing a US rebuke of 'terror'
cards.what_happened: For **five consecutive nights**, dozens of Israeli settlers encircled three Palestinian homes on the edge of Qusra, pitching tents outside and cutting off the residents' water and electricity, forcing families to drink from a well as supplies ran low. Israeli troops eventually moved in and said they dismantled **two illegal outposts** near the town, detaining one Israeli settler, but were met by more settlers who rolled boulders into the road and threw rocks; soldiers responded with sound grenades and pepper spray before pulling back. **US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee** — normally a strong defender of Israel's government — broke with that pattern and called the siege a **'horrific act of terror.'** In the aftermath, a mosque in Qusra was set on fire and the Hebrew word for **'revenge'** was found spray-painted on its wall, according to CNN and the Washington Post.
key_points: Israeli settlers surrounded **three Palestinian homes** near Qusra for **five straight nights**, cutting water and power.
The **US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee**, called the siege a **'horrific act of terror.'**
Israeli troops dismantled **two illegal outposts** but were pelted with rocks by settlers who kept arriving.
The **UN** says Qusra saw **more settler attacks than any other West Bank community** in 2026.
A mosque in Qusra was set on fire, with **'revenge'** spray-painted on its wall in Hebrew.

depth.background: The West Bank is Palestinian territory that Israel has occupied since 1967; roughly 500,000 Israeli settlers now live there in communities most of the world considers illegal under international law, alongside about 3 million Palestinians. Settler violence against Palestinian villages has been rising for years, often carried out by small groups who set up unauthorized outposts and try to force Palestinian families off land they've lived on for generations. **Qusra**, a town of a few thousand people, has become one of the worst-hit places, recording more settler attacks than anywhere else in the West Bank this year according to the UN. Israel's military is legally responsible for protecting Palestinian civilians there, which is why the length of this siege — and the slow response — drew such sharp international criticism.

cards.title: A new study finds the speed of global warming — not just its final level — decides whether a critical Atlantic current collapses
cards.what_happened: Researchers at **Utrecht University** ran climate simulations testing what happens to the AMOC under different warming speeds, not just different warming totals. They found that when CO2-driven warming happens **rapidly, the AMOC can collapse at around 2°C** of global warming — a threshold the world could cross within decades on current trends. But when the same amount of warming happens **slowly, the ocean has time to adapt**, and the current can stay stable even past **5°C**. The study, published in the journal **Nature Climate Change**, argues that the rate of change matters as much as the final temperature target. This matters directly for climate policy: many plans, including elements tied to the Paris Agreement, assume it's acceptable to temporarily 'overshoot' a temperature target as long as it's brought back down later — this research suggests that overshoot strategy could be far riskier than assumed if the overshoot happens fast.
key_points: Dutch researchers found that **rapid warming can collapse the AMOC current at just 2°C**, while slow warming lets it survive **past 5°C**.
The AMOC is the ocean current system that carries **warm tropical water north**, keeping Western Europe's climate mild.
The study, from **Utrecht University**, was published in **Nature Climate Change**.
It challenges climate policy built around **'overshoot' pathways** that assume peak warming can be temporary.
A collapsed AMOC would bring **much colder winters to Europe** and disrupt weather patterns worldwide.

depth.background: The **Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC)** is a system of ocean currents — including the Gulf Stream — that carries warm water from the tropics up toward Europe and the Arctic, then sends cooler, denser water back south at depth, like a giant conveyor belt. It's a major reason Western Europe is milder than other places at the same latitude (like parts of Canada). Scientists have warned for years that melting ice and warming oceans could weaken or even shut this system down, and past studies have disagreed on how close that tipping point actually is. This new research adds a twist: it's not just how hot the planet gets, but how fast it gets there, that determines whether the AMOC survives.

cards.title: Wall Street's S&P 500 closes at a fresh record as cooling inflation and falling oil prices lift stocks
cards.what_happened: On Thursday, fresh US inflation data came in **softer than economists expected**, easing fears that the Fed would need to keep rates high for longer. At the same time, oil prices retreated from their recent spike, taking pressure off transport and energy costs that feed into broader inflation. Together, the two moves pushed the **S&P 500 to a new closing record of 7,798.99**, a 0.7% gain, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 69.72 points (0.13%) to 53,839.99 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.81% to 26,803.03. It marks the second time in roughly a week the S&P has set a fresh all-time high.
key_points: The **S&P 500** closed at a record **7,798.99**, up 0.7% on the day.
The **Dow Jones** rose to **53,839.99** and the **Nasdaq** gained 0.8% to **26,803.03**.
The rally was driven by a **cooler-than-expected US inflation report** and **falling oil prices**.
It is the index's second fresh record in two weeks, extending a **booming 2026 rally**.

depth.background: US stocks have been on a strong run through 2026, helped by a Federal Reserve under new chair **Kevin Warsh** that has kept interest rates steady even as some officials push for hikes. Inflation — the pace at which prices for everyday goods rise — has been the market's biggest worry all year, because faster inflation usually means higher interest rates, which make borrowing costlier for companies and consumers alike. Oil prices have also been volatile because of the standoff over the **Strait of Hormuz**, a narrow shipping chokepoint that carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil.

cards.title: A federal judge presses the Trump DOJ to explain why it's still withholding parts of the Epstein files
cards.what_happened: On Thursday, US District Judge **Emmet Sullivan** held a hearing pressing DOJ lawyers, led by Attorney General **Todd Blanche**, to explain why certain material remains redacted or withheld months after the transparency law took effect. The hearing stems from a lawsuit filed by an independent journalist alleging the DOJ's redactions and withholdings are unlawful; in **June**, Sullivan had already found some of the department's withholding violated the Act. Separately, another federal judge in New York, **Loretta Preska**, ruled this week that a batch of previously undisclosed Epstein-related documents can be made public, rejecting arguments from Epstein associate **Ghislaine Maxwell** that they should remain sealed.
key_points: A **federal judge** ordered DOJ officials to justify redactions in the Jeffrey Epstein files in court.
Attorney General **Todd Blanche** had to explain the department's refusal to unredact certain material.
The judge had already ruled in **June** that some withheld material violates the **Epstein Files Transparency Act**.
Withheld notes reportedly include material involving **allegations against President Trump**.
A separate ruling this week cleared other Epstein-related documents for release over Ghislaine Maxwell's objections.

depth.background: Congress passed the **Epstein Files Transparency Act** requiring the Justice Department to release investigative files related to the late financier and convicted sex offender **Jeffrey Epstein**, who died in 2019 while facing federal sex-trafficking charges. The law followed years of public pressure over what the government knew, and who else may have been implicated in Epstein's abuse network. Since the law passed, the DOJ has released millions of pages, but plaintiffs and journalists say officials have redacted or withheld material without adequate legal justification, including notes that reportedly reference the president.

cards.title: Israel says it won't leave southern Lebanon until Hezbollah disarms, walking back talk of indefinite occupation
cards.what_happened: On **August 12**, Israel's defense minister suggested Israeli forces could stay in southern Lebanon indefinitely, a comment that drew swift criticism from Washington for undercutting the framework deal it had brokered. A day later, on **August 13**, he qualified those remarks, saying Israel will withdraw — but only once Hezbollah is disarmed, not on a fixed timeline. Under the pilot program linked to the framework, Israeli forces are only slated to pull back from the zone between the **Yellow Line and the Litani River**, not from all of Israel's security positions in Lebanon. Lebanon's government, for its part, has struggled to convince or compel Hezbollah to hand over weapons it says it needs for deterrence.
key_points: Israel's defense minister said troops stay until Hezbollah is **fully disarmed**, walking back a remark a day earlier that had implied indefinite occupation
The retreat from those remarks came after **direct criticism from the US**, which brokered the underlying deal
A **June 26 framework agreement** ties any Israeli withdrawal to the Lebanese army removing Hezbollah's weapons
A pilot pullback covers only the strip between the **Yellow Line and the Litani River** — a partial, not full, withdrawal
Hezbollah, badly weakened in its 2024 war with Israel, has so far resisted giving up its arsenal

depth.background: Hezbollah is a heavily armed, Iran-backed political and militant movement based in Lebanon that has fought several wars with Israel since the 1980s. After a bruising 2024 conflict badly damaged Hezbollah's leadership and arsenal, the US brokered a **June 26, 2026 framework agreement**: Israeli troops would gradually leave southern Lebanon as the Lebanese national army verifiably disarmed Hezbollah and other non-state militias. Israel has occupied parts of southern Lebanon on and off for decades, arguing it needs a buffer zone to stop cross-border attacks. The disarmament process has moved slowly, leaving Israeli troops still present well past early informal deadlines.

cards.title: Russia says it's ready to resume Ukraine peace talks — but only to discuss Washington's plan, not a multi-party one
cards.what_happened: Grigory Karasin, chairman of the Russian Federation Council's foreign affairs committee, said Thursday that Russia is ready to resume peace talks on ending the war in Ukraine. He specified that Moscow's negotiators are prepared to discuss the **new proposals brought by the US**, and see **no obstacles** to a meeting with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Karasin added a pointed condition: Russia wants to consider proposals **from one side — Washington — rather than a combined plan from multiple parties**, an apparent swipe at attempts to bring Ukraine and European governments into the same drafting process. The statement doesn't set a date or format for any meeting, and doesn't walk back Russia's core demand that Ukraine hand over the remainder of the Donbas region it still controls, a demand Kyiv has repeatedly rejected. It comes after weeks in which Russian officials, including Lavrov, downplayed the urgency of a return to the table.
key_points: Grigory Karasin, who chairs the Russian upper house's foreign affairs committee, says Moscow has **no obstacles** to meeting US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
The catch: Russia wants to discuss **only the new US proposals**, not a plan negotiated with Ukraine and Europe at the table too.
This follows months where Russia's chief negotiators played down or stalled on restarting talks entirely.
No date or venue has been confirmed yet for any Witkoff-Kushner meeting with Russian officials.
Russia's underlying territorial demand — that Ukraine cede the rest of Donbas — has **not changed**.

depth.background: The US has been running a parallel diplomatic track to the stalled Istanbul-framework talks, with **Steve Witkoff** (Trump's special envoy) and **Jared Kushner** shuttling proposals between Washington, Kyiv and Moscow. Russia spent much of the summer signaling it was in no rush to talk, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov repeatedly rejecting a front-line freeze as a precondition. Ukraine, meanwhile, has said it's ready to talk but needs clarity on what the Kremlin's actual terms are, since Russian officials have often floated different demands in different forums. **Karasin's comments** are the clearest recent signal that Moscow sees the direct Washington-run channel, not a broader multilateral one, as the venue it's willing to use.

cards.title: Taiwan deliberately slowed mobile internet for 16 million people to rehearse for a Chinese invasion
cards.what_happened: On Thursday, Taiwanese telecom operators throttled mobile internet speeds down to **256 Kbps** — slow enough that only basic texting works, not video or most apps — across seven northern jurisdictions including Taipei, New Taipei City, and Keelung, from 2:30 to 3:00pm local time. This was the second of two throttling phases run as part of **Han Kuang 42**, Taiwan's largest annual military exercise, which ran from August 5 to 14 this year. Combined, the two throttling phases affected roughly **16 million people**, about 70% of Taiwan's total population. The **Taiwan Stock Exchange** was granted an exemption so trading wasn't disrupted. President **Lai Ching-te** publicly apologized for the inconvenience, telling residents 'we ask for your understanding and support, as this is a necessary drill.' The exercise is explicitly designed to model how the island would cope if China attempted an invasion or blockade and tried to cut off communications.
key_points: Telecom carriers throttled mobile data to **256 Kbps** — barely enough for text messages — across two rounds covering **~16 million people**, about **70% of Taiwan's population**.
The second throttle hit **seven jurisdictions in northern Taiwan**, including Taipei, from 2:30-3:00pm local time on Thursday.
It's the final phase of **Han Kuang 42**, Taiwan's largest annual military exercise, which ran August 5-14.
President **Lai Ching-te** personally apologized for the inconvenience, calling it a 'necessary drill.'
The goal: test whether civilians and businesses can still function if China knocks out or jams normal telecom networks during an invasion or blockade.

depth.background: **Han Kuang** is Taiwan's flagship annual exercise simulating a Chinese invasion, and it has grown more elaborate each year as tensions with **Beijing** have escalated — China claims Taiwan as its own territory and has not ruled out taking it by force. Past editions focused mostly on military maneuvers; this year added a large-scale **civilian resilience** component, testing whether ordinary people, hospitals, and businesses could keep functioning if China's real war plan includes disabling or jamming Taiwan's communications networks, a tactic seen in other modern conflicts. The drill deliberately picked telecom infrastructure because a full communications blackout is considered one of the most disruptive opening moves an attacker could make.

prev_ref.title: Iran says the Strait of Hormuz is still shut despite Trump's claims, as tanker traffic sinks to a one-week low

cards.title: Tankers are attacked and an oil spill spreads in the Strait of Hormuz, as Trump and Iran trade claims over who controls it
cards.what_happened: On Thursday evening, two tankers belonging to the UAE's state oil company ADNOC were attacked while transiting the Strait; no one was hurt and the vessels remained under control. Separately, the oil slick from the sunken Russian shadow-fleet tanker has now spread across an estimated **500 square miles**, threatening coastlines and shipping lanes. Commercial traffic through the Strait sank to just eight vessels tracked in the past week, a fraction of normal volumes. President Trump said the US has 'total control' over the Strait and suggested Washington 'might keep it', while Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned the US to 'be careful', calling Trump's claim 'fake intelligence'. Iran maintains the Strait is under its own military supervision and that no vessel can pass without its permission.
key_points: Two Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (**ADNOC**) tankers were attacked while transiting the Strait on **Thursday evening**; no injuries were reported.
An oil spill from a Russian 'shadow fleet' tanker that sank off Oman has now spread across roughly **500 square miles** of sea.
Traffic through the Strait has fallen to a one-week low of just **eight vessels**, versus dozens normally.
Trump claims the **US has 'total control'** of the Strait and might 'keep it'; Iran's foreign minister told him to 'be careful'.
Iran insists the waterway is under its **'complete management and control'** and that no ship can pass without its permission.

thread.previously: We reported Iran was keeping the Strait effectively closed despite Trump's claims that it remained open, with tanker traffic already sinking to a one-week low.
thread.changed: Two ADNOC tankers were now directly attacked in the Strait, the Oman oil spill has grown to roughly 500 square miles, and Trump has escalated by claiming the US has 'total control' of the waterway — prompting a sharp warning from Iran's foreign minister.

depth.background: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow chokepoint between Iran and Oman that roughly **a fifth of the world's oil** normally passes through on its way from Gulf producers to global markets. Since a US-Iran conflict escalated this summer, Iran has restricted shipping through the Strait and a sanctioned Russian 'shadow fleet' tanker — an aging, often uninsured ship used to move oil around Western sanctions — sank nearby, spilling crude. The US has responded by asserting it now effectively controls the waterway, a claim Tehran rejects.

prev_ref.title: Colombia's earthquake toll climbs past 265 as more than 2,700 remain reported missing

cards.title: Colombia's earthquake death toll rises to 273 as rescuers enter a 'final phase' — but the missing count drops sharply as thousands are found
cards.what_happened: Colombia's disaster-management agency says the confirmed death toll has climbed to **273**, with 3,824 injured, as of the latest count. Crucially, the number of people still classified as missing has fallen dramatically — from more than 2,700 reported missing earlier in the week to **377** now — as search teams worked through the rubble and located thousands of previously unaccounted-for residents. One notable rescue: a 32-year-old woman was pulled out alive in Pereira after more than 36 hours trapped. Authorities say rescue operations have now entered their 'final phase', with international help including roughly 40 US search-and-rescue personnel. The quake damaged over 200 roads, five airports, and 44 water systems (aqueducts) across the affected region.
key_points: The death toll from Colombia's **7.4-magnitude earthquake** has risen to **273**, with **3,824** people reported injured.
The number still listed as missing has fallen sharply to **377**, down from over 2,700 reported missing days earlier, as many were located.
A **32-year-old woman was pulled alive** from rubble in Pereira after being trapped for more than **36 hours**.
Rescue operations have entered a **'final phase'**, with US urban search-and-rescue teams (~40 people) helping local first responders.
More than **200 roads**, 5 airports, and 44 aqueducts were damaged, hitting the hard-hit Pereira and Cali regions.

thread.previously: We reported the death toll had passed 265 with over 2,700 people still reported missing, as rescue teams struggled to reach the earthquake's epicenter.
thread.changed: The death toll has risen only modestly to 273, but the missing count has collapsed to 377 as thousands were located — and officials now say rescue operations are entering their 'final phase'.

depth.background: A 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia on **August 10**, centered near San José del Palmar in Chocó department — the country's strongest quake in a century. It flattened buildings and infrastructure across the Pereira and Cali regions, triggering a mass rescue operation. Colombia's new government faced criticism over aid access and the pace of the response in the disaster's first days.

cards.title: Astronomers using the James Webb telescope find a brand-new kind of cosmic object: a 'black hole star'
cards.what_happened: MIT-led astronomers spotted an unusually bright red dot in one of the deepest images JWST has ever taken, dating to just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang. The object looked like an enormous star — physically about the size of our solar system — but was radiating **100 billion times more energy** than any known star could physically generate. After ruling out other explanations, the team concluded the most likely answer is a hybrid never seen before: a **black hole embedded inside a giant envelope of hydrogen gas**, acting almost like the black hole is 'wearing' a star. They estimate the black hole at its centre is about **100,000 times the mass of the Sun**. The team has named the object MoM-BH*-1 and published the analysis in Nature. If the interpretation holds up under further observation, it would be the first confirmed example of an entirely new astrophysical category.
key_points: A team led by MIT found an object glowing with **100 billion times** more energy than any known star can produce.
It's a **supermassive black hole** (about 100,000 times the Sun's mass) wrapped in a hydrogen envelope roughly the size of our solar system.
Spotted by the **James Webb Space Telescope** just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang — one of the earliest objects ever seen.
Nicknamed **'MoM-BH*-1'**, it could explain how supermassive black holes grew so fast in the universe's infancy.
The findings were published in the journal **Nature**, and the team calls it a genuinely new class of object.

depth.background: Astronomers have long been puzzled by how **supermassive black holes** — the kind that sit at the centre of galaxies, including our own — managed to grow so enormous so quickly after the Big Bang. Normal black hole growth, where a black hole slowly swallows nearby gas and stars, is thought to be too slow to explain black holes this size existing only a few hundred million years into the universe's 13.8-billion-year history. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, was built partly to peer further back in time than any previous telescope, letting scientists directly observe this early era for the first time. Its 'Mirage or Miracle' survey — designed to hunt for exactly these kinds of puzzling early-universe objects — is what turned up this find.

cards.title: Canada and the US race to strike a trade deal before Washington's Aug. 19 deadline for 50% tariffs
cards.what_happened: Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and chief negotiator Janice Charette met US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Washington on Thursday, Aug. 13 — their second sit-down with Greer this week, part of a run of meetings that has kept them in Washington since Monday. The talks are racing against an **Aug. 19 deadline**, after which the US is set to impose **50% tariffs** on about **$20 billion** worth of Canadian exports, covering goods like alcohol, hockey sticks, and cement. Crucially, these tariffs would carry no exemption for goods that already comply with CUSMA — unlike most of Trump's other tariff actions. Greer has said the tariffs respond to three things: provincial bans on US liquor, Canada's retaliatory tariffs on US vehicles and parts, and Canada's dairy quota system, which Washington says treats US dairy worse than the EU gets under a separate deal. Canadian officials are reportedly prepared to lift the alcohol bans and offer concessions on autos and dairy in exchange for tariff relief, hoping to have a deal framework ready to show Trump before next Wednesday. PM Mark Carney has called the talks "constructive" but says Canada "will not accept a bad deal," keeping retaliation on the table if talks collapse.
key_points: Canada's trade minister met the US Trade Representative in Washington for the **second time this week**, six days before a hard deadline.
Without a deal, the US will impose **50% tariffs** on roughly **$20 billion** of Canadian exports — including alcohol, hockey sticks, and cement — starting **Aug. 19**.
Unlike most other Trump tariffs, these come with **no exemption** for goods that comply with the existing US-Canada-Mexico trade agreement (CUSMA).
Washington's three complaints: **provincial bans on US alcohol**, Canada's retaliatory **auto tariffs**, and its **dairy quota system**.
Canada is reportedly ready to **drop the alcohol bans** and ease auto/dairy barriers for relief, though PM Mark Carney says he **won't accept a bad deal**.

depth.background: Trump has used tariff threats repeatedly this year as leverage in trade disputes, and Canada has been a repeated target despite the two countries' deep trade ties and the existing free-trade deal, **CUSMA** (the Canada-US-Mexico Agreement, the successor to NAFTA). Most Canadian provinces — every one except Alberta and Saskatchewan — pulled American alcohol from liquor-store shelves earlier this year in retaliation for previous Trump tariffs, which the US now cites as a grievance. Canada, in turn, has its own retaliatory tariffs on US-made vehicles and parts, and a dairy quota system that limits US dairy access — both now also on Washington's complaint list.

cards.title: Sudan's RSF hits Khartoum with drones for a second straight day, as El Obeid comes under renewed assault
cards.what_happened: On Thursday, Sudanese army air-defence units intercepted a second consecutive day of RSF drone attacks aimed at Khartoum, shooting down multiple suicide drones approaching from the west over northern and western Omdurman, one of the three cities that make up greater Khartoum. Witnesses reported anti-aircraft fire and explosions as the drones were engaged. The attacks followed a Wednesday barrage that hit Omdurman, Atbara (in River Nile state), and **El Obeid**, the capital of North Kordofan — where falling drone debris **killed two people** and eight separate drones were aimed at the city, triggering army air defenses there too. No group has formally claimed the strikes, but they are widely attributed to the RSF, which has increasingly relied on drones as it has lost ground in direct combat. The escalation comes as the RSF appears to be probing El Obeid, one of the last army-held cities standing between RSF-controlled Darfur and the government's central Sudan strongholds.
key_points: Sudanese army air-defence units shot down multiple **RSF suicide drones** over Omdurman on **Thursday**, the second straight day of strikes on the capital.
Wednesday's barrage hit **three cities at once** — Omdurman, Atbara, and El Obeid — where falling drone debris **killed two people**.
El Obeid, capital of **North Kordofan**, is the next major army-held city the RSF appears to be probing after capturing **El Fasher** in October 2025.
The UN says at least **6,000 people were killed in three days** when El Fasher fell; some researchers estimate the true toll may be as high as **150,000**.
Roughly **24.6 million people** in Sudan face acute hunger, with **2 million** at risk of outright famine.

depth.background: Sudan's civil war has raged since April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (the army) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group that grew out of the Darfur-era Janjaweed militias. The RSF's biggest recent victory came in October 2025 when it captured **El Fasher**, the army's last major stronghold in Darfur, after an 18-month siege — a takeover now regarded as one of the deadliest events of the war, with rights groups raising the possibility of genocide given the ethnic-targeting pattern of the killings. With Darfur effectively under RSF control, fighting has shifted east toward Kordofan and the capital region. **El Obeid**, capital of North Kordofan, sits on the road between RSF-held Darfur and army-held central Sudan, making it the next logical target.

prev_ref.title: Houthi rebels kill 11 in Yemen's Mokha and strike a Saudi Aramco refinery as the Red Sea conflict reignites

cards.title: Houthi forces launch their biggest ground offensive since 2022, raising fears Yemen could slide back into civil war
cards.what_happened: Since roughly **August 6**, Houthi forces have escalated ground attacks against Saudi-backed Yemeni government positions on multiple fronts, including **Taiz and Marib**, killing at least **30 government troops** in the initial wave. Government forces say they repelled a fresh Houthi assault today on the al-Mafalis front, south of Haifan in Taiz province. This follows Tuesday's separate Houthi strike on the port of Mokha and a Saudi Aramco refinery, which killed 11 people. Analysts describe this as the most substantial Houthi military campaign since the 2022 UN-brokered truce, and warn Yemen risks sliding back into full civil war after years of frozen conflict. Saudi Arabia has so far held back from committing its own troops, but has responded diplomatically: it announced a 13-country Red Sea maritime security coalition on July 30 and signed new defense pacts with Pakistan and Turkey on August 7.
key_points: Houthi forces have launched their **biggest offensive since a 2022 truce** paused Yemen's eight-year civil war.
At least **30 government troops** were killed in the opening wave of attacks around **Taiz and Marib**.
Yemeni government forces say they repelled a fresh Houthi attack on the **al-Mafalis front** south of Haifan today.
Cambridge analyst **Elisabeth Kendall** warns a full relapse into civil war is now a 'looming possibility.'
Saudi Arabia hasn't sent troops but has signed new **defense pacts with Pakistan and Turkey** and formed a 13-country Red Sea maritime coalition.

thread.previously: On August 11 we reported that Iran-backed Houthi rebels killed 11 people in a strike on Yemen's port city of Mokha and hit a Saudi Aramco refinery, reigniting the Red Sea conflict after roughly a year of relative calm.
thread.changed: The fighting has now spread from the coast to the ground: since around August 6, Houthi forces have pushed a multi-front offensive against Saudi-backed Yemeni government troops around Taiz and Marib, killing at least 30 government soldiers in the opening wave. Analysts call it the most serious Houthi campaign since the 2022 truce that paused Yemen's civil war, and warn a full relapse into war is now a real possibility.

depth.background: Yemen's civil war has run since **2014**, pitting the Iran-backed Houthi movement — which controls the capital Sanaa and much of the north — against an internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government. A **UN-brokered truce in 2022** froze the front lines and mostly held for years, even as the Houthis separately attacked Red Sea shipping over the Gaza war. That fragile calm cracked on August 11 when Houthi forces struck Yemen's port city of Mokha and a Saudi Aramco refinery, killing 11 — the first fatal Red Sea attack in over a year. The ground war has now reignited too.

cards.title: US senators demand answers after sailors try to jump off the USS Abraham Lincoln during a record-length deployment
cards.what_happened: Sailors and Marines aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln have now been at sea for **more than 260 days**, with **over 200 days** since the ship's last port call — believed to be the longest stretch without shore leave for a US carrier in the modern era. Family members and unnamed crew have told reporters that multiple sailors have either attempted to go overboard or been physically restrained before they could. One family described a sailor texting that '**he hopes he doesn't wake up tomorrow**.' The ship was originally meant to return home months ago but was instead extended and redirected toward the Middle East as part of the US military posture around Iran and the Strait of Hormuz. Democratic senators Ruben Gallego and Richard Blumenthal are now demanding the Navy grant Congress an oversight visit and provide a full accounting of overboard and self-harm incidents by **August 27**. The Navy has so far declined to confirm exact numbers, and it's unclear when the strike group will finally return to port.
key_points: The **USS Abraham Lincoln** carrier strike group has been at sea for **more than 260 days**, without a single port call in over **200 days** — a modern-day record.
Multiple sailors have reportedly tried to **jump overboard**, with families describing crew texting that they 'hope they don't wake up tomorrow.'
The ship, carrying roughly **5,000 sailors and Marines**, was diverted from a routine Pacific deployment to the Middle East for Iran-related operations.
Democratic senators **Ruben Gallego and Richard Blumenthal** are demanding a congressional oversight visit and Navy answers by **August 27**.
The Navy has not confirmed how many overboard or self-harm incidents have actually occurred.

depth.background: The USS Abraham Lincoln and its strike group left San Diego on **November 21, 2025**, on what was originally billed as a standard Pacific deployment. As tensions over the **Strait of Hormuz** and Iran escalated through 2026, the Navy redirected the carrier to the Middle East instead of bringing it home. US Navy deployments are typically capped around six to seven months precisely because extended time at sea erodes crew welfare — mental health, family strain, and morale all suffer the longer a ship stays out. This deployment has now blown past that norm by months, with no announced return date.

cards.title: A data center operator is exploring a $100 billion IPO — a sign of how big the AI building boom has gotten
cards.what_happened: According to people familiar with the matter, **Vantage Data Centers** has held preliminary discussions in recent weeks about possible exit paths for its private-equity owners, meeting informally with financial advisers about a stock market listing or a sale. An **IPO** could value the company at around **$100 billion** and raise roughly **$10 billion** for the business — a figure that would make it the largest-ever data center IPO. The company is also weighing a sale, including selling a stake to new investors, as an alternative route. Any deal remains at an early, non-binding stage, and could happen as soon as next year if it proceeds. The exploration comes as AI-driven demand for computing power keeps pushing valuations for data-center operators sharply higher.
key_points: **Vantage Data Centers** is exploring an IPO that could value it at roughly **$100 billion**, which would make it the largest data-center listing ever
The company, backed by private equity firm **Silver Lake** and infrastructure investor **DigitalBridge**, could raise around **$10 billion** in the offering
A **sale**, including a partial stake sale, is also being considered as an alternative to going public
Talks are still preliminary — no formal process has launched, and timing, size, and structure could all change
Vantage has already raised roughly **$11 billion** since late 2023 to build out data centers, underscoring how much capital the AI infrastructure race is consuming

depth.background: **Data centers** are the physical warehouses full of servers and specialized chips (like Nvidia's GPUs) that actually run AI models — every ChatGPT-style answer or AI image is computed inside one. As AI demand has exploded, so has the need for these facilities, and the private equity and infrastructure firms that own them have been pouring in tens of billions of dollars to build bigger ones, faster. Vantage Data Centers is one of the largest such operators globally, and its owners — Silver Lake and DigitalBridge — have already put in over **$9 billion** in equity since 2023 to fund its expansion.

prev_ref.title: A total solar eclipse sweeps across mainland Europe for the first time since 1999

cards.title: Spain just had its first total solar eclipse since 1905 — and it's only the opener in an unheard-of three-eclipse run through 2028
cards.what_happened: On Wednesday, the Moon's shadow swept from **Greenland and Iceland across northern Spain** as the Sun set, delivering totality — the brief window when the Moon fully blocks the Sun — to an estimated **15 million people**, most of them in Spain. It was the **first total solar eclipse over mainland Europe since 1999** and mainland Spain's first since **1905**. Scientists used the rare darkness to study the Sun's **corona**, the outer atmosphere normally invisible in daylight, which affects space weather that can disrupt satellites and power grids. What makes this moment bigger than a single afternoon is the calendar that follows: Spain will see a second total eclipse on **August 2, 2027**, then an annular eclipse on **January 26, 2028** — a three-eclipse sequence astronomers are calling the 'Iberian trio', the first cluster of total eclipses over mainland Europe this century.
key_points: Monday's eclipse was Spain's first total solar eclipse in mainland territory since **1905** — 121 years.
A second total eclipse will cross Spain again on **August 2, 2027**, visible from the Iberian Peninsula down into North Africa and the Middle East.
A third eclipse — an **annular** ('ring of fire') eclipse where the Moon doesn't fully cover the Sun — follows on **January 26, 2028**.
Astronomers are calling it the **'Iberian trio'**, an occurrence so rare that few countries have experienced three eclipses this close together.
The totality path this week reached as far as **Palma, Valencia, Zaragoza, Bilbao and León**, with observers getting up to 1 minute 50 seconds of darkness.

thread.previously: We covered Tuesday's eclipse as it happened: totality began around 15:34 GMT and swept from Iceland to Spain, lasting up to 2 minutes 18 seconds, watched by an estimated 15 million people, and coinciding with the Perseid meteor shower.
thread.changed: Now that the event has passed, the bigger story is emerging: this wasn't a one-off. It's the first of **three consecutive total or annular solar eclipses to cross Spain by 2028** — a concentration of eclipses astronomers say almost no country has ever seen in such a short span, turning Spain into a hub for eclipse tourism for the rest of the decade.

depth.background: Total solar eclipses happen somewhere on Earth every year or two, but any single spot on the planet typically waits **centuries** between them, because the Moon's shadow is only about 100 miles wide and sweeps across a thin, fast-moving path. Mainland Spain's last one was in **1905**; mainland Europe as a whole hadn't seen one since **1999**. That's what made this week's event, and the discovery that two more are coming within two years, so unusual to scientists who track these cycles.

prev_ref.title: Colombia's 72-hour rescue window closes as the toll passes 220 and aid refusals spark backlash

cards.title: Colombia's earthquake toll climbs past 265 as more than 2,700 remain reported missing
