cards.title: England bowl Pakistan out for 171 on a rain-hit opening day at Headingley, piling pressure on a fragile batting line-up
cards.what_happened: On a rain-disrupted opening day at Headingley, England **bowled Pakistan out for just 171 runs**, with seamers **Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue combining for 10 wickets** to rip through the batting line-up. England then reached **112 for 2** in their reply by the close of play, already building a commanding position in the match despite the interrupted overs. The collapse extends a pattern of fragile batting performances that has plagued Pakistan's Test side through this difficult stretch, adding fresh scrutiny to the team just as it tries to stabilize under restored leadership.
key_points: Pakistan were bowled out for just **171** on the rain-interrupted opening day of the first Test at Headingley.
England seamers **Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue shared 10 wickets** between them.
England closed the day at **112 for 2** in reply, already well ahead in the match.
Play was repeatedly interrupted by rain, compressing the day's overs.
The result deepens the pressure on Pakistan's batting after a build-up already clouded by fitness and form concerns.
cards.moot: Restoring a familiar face to leadership doesn't fix underlying structural problems on its own — a team's deeper issues, like a fragile batting order, still have to be solved on the field, one innings at a time.

thread.previously: We reported that England and Pakistan were starting a three-Test series at Headingley with two comeback captains, Joe Root and Babar Azam, both trying to stabilize teams that had been through recent turmoil, with Babar only just cleared to play after a hand injury.
thread.changed: Play has now happened — England bowled Pakistan out for 171 thanks to Robinson and Tongue's 10 combined wickets, and reached 112 for 2 in reply, putting England firmly on top after a rain-hit first day.

depth.background: England and Pakistan are playing the first of a **three-Test series** at Headingley in Leeds, with both sides entering out of form — Pakistan sit eighth in the World Test Championship table with only two wins in six matches, while England, seventh, are coming off a home series loss to New Zealand. **Joe Root** is captaining England for the first time since giving up the role in 2022, and **Babar Azam** returned as Pakistan's Test captain after being restored to the role, having been cleared to play despite a hand injury picked up in a warm-up match. Both boards are betting that bringing back experienced former captains can stabilize teams that have each been through recent turmoil.
depth.why_it_matters: This isn't just one bad day — it's the latest data point in a longer pattern of Pakistan's batting collapsing under pressure, which is exactly the kind of instability their board hoped restoring experienced leadership would fix.
depth.ripple_effects: A heavy defeat here would pile more pressure on Pakistan's team management and selection decisions heading into the rest of the series. It also strengthens England's position early in a series both teams needed to use as a form-finding opportunity.
depth.why_now: This is the direct follow-through on the series opener we flagged yesterday — the first day of play has now delivered a concrete result that starts answering which team's leadership reset is actually working.
depth.watch_next: Whether Pakistan can respond with the bat in their second innings, or whether the collapse repeats and hands England a dominant series lead.

cards.title: BCCI faces a repeat trophy standoff with ACC chief Mohsin Naqvi as the Women's Asia Cup nears, with India's men's trophy still unclaimed
cards.what_happened: With the **Women's Asia Cup 2026** set to run from **August 28 to September 13** in Dubai, cricket administrators are already bracing for a repeat of last year's men's trophy standoff if **Harmanpreet Kaur's** defending-champion India side wins the title. The men's Asia Cup trophy from last year's final — which India's team refused to accept directly from Naqvi, also skipping handshakes with Pakistan's players and the presentation ceremony — has still not been formally handed over to India more than a year later. One proposed solution being discussed is for Naqvi to step aside from the presentation duties and let another ACC official hand over any trophy India might win this time, but the BCCI has not publicly stated whether it would even accept a trophy in a ceremony involving Naqvi at all.
key_points: The **Women's Asia Cup 2026** runs **August 28 to September 13** in Dubai, and could revive last year's India-Naqvi trophy standoff if India's women win.
In last year's **men's Asia Cup final**, India's team refused to accept the trophy from **Mohsin Naqvi**, skipped the presentation, and declined handshakes with Pakistan's players.
That men's trophy has **still not been handed over to India**, more than a year later.
One proposed workaround has **Naqvi step aside** and let another ACC official present the trophy instead.
The **BCCI has not revealed** its position on whether it would accept a trophy from Naqvi if India's women win this time.
cards.moot: In sport, ceremonial moments aren't just formalities — when political relationships between countries are strained, even a trophy handover can become a deliberate, high-visibility statement.

depth.background: **Mohsin Naqvi** is both Pakistan's interior minister and the president of the **Asian Cricket Council (ACC)**, the body that governs cricket across Asia and runs the Asia Cup. India and Pakistan's cricket rivalry is unusually fraught because the two countries don't play bilateral cricket outside ICC and ACC events, given broader political tensions, which means moments like trophy presentations become rare, highly charged flashpoints. Last year, after India's men beat Pakistan in the Asia Cup final in Dubai, the India team led by Suryakumar Yadav refused to accept the trophy from Naqvi and skipped the podium ceremony entirely — an unprecedented snub that left the trophy in limbo.
depth.why_it_matters: This shows how India-Pakistan political tension routinely spills directly into cricket's biggest ceremonial moments, turning something as simple as a trophy handover into a diplomatic flashpoint that can overshadow the sport itself.
depth.ripple_effects: A repeat standoff would put the ACC in an awkward position as the body trying to govern cricket across a region where two of its biggest members won't directly engage with each other. It also keeps pressure on cricket boards to find protocol workarounds for future India-Pakistan matchups in any format.
depth.why_now: The Women's Asia Cup starting August 28 is close enough that administrators and reporters are now actively discussing how to avoid a repeat of last year's unresolved standoff before it happens again.
depth.watch_next: Whether the ACC formally confirms a Naqvi-free presentation protocol before the tournament begins, and whether India's women's team ends up in the final against Pakistan or as champions at all.

key_terms.definition: The regional body that governs cricket across Asia and organizes tournaments like the Asia Cup, separate from the global International Cricket Council (ICC).

cards.title: Pakistan's latest batting collapse puts stand-in captain Salman Agha's leadership under the microscope
cards.what_happened: On the opening day of the first Test at Headingley, Pakistan looked settled after **Abdullah Shafique and Imam-ul-Haq** put on **91 runs** together — the only real resistance of the innings — before the middle and lower order collapsed, losing their last **eight wickets for just 74 runs** to be bowled out for **171** in 48.1 overs. England's seamers **Ollie Robinson** and **Josh Tongue** took five wickets apiece, exploiting conditions that, while difficult, were described by observers as not unplayable. England responded by reaching **112 for 2** by the close of a rain-affected day, taking firm control of the match. The collapse immediately became the story of the day, with observers noting Pakistan's now-familiar pattern of promising partnerships undone by sudden capitulations, unfolding under a stand-in captain thrust into the role by injury.
key_points: Pakistan collapsed from a promising **91-run partnership** to being bowled out for just **171** on day one at Headingley, losing their **last 8 wickets for 74 runs**.
**Salman Ali Agha** is standing in as captain after **Babar Azam** was ruled out with a hand injury, putting him in charge for a must-not-lose opener.
England's **Ollie Robinson (5/51)** and **Josh Tongue (5/46)** did the damage, bowling Pakistan out in just **48.1 overs**.
It's the latest in a pattern: Pakistan were also routed by **Bangladesh** and have struggled repeatedly against high-quality pace bowling overseas this year.
England closed day one at **112/2**, already in firm control of the match.
cards.moot: A single innings collapse rarely happens in isolation — when the same team keeps losing wickets in clusters against good bowling, it usually points to a deeper pattern in technique or temperament that one good partnership can't paper over.

depth.background: Pakistan's Test side has been searching for stability all year, cycling through injury absences and leadership changes while struggling against quality seam bowling away from home. Babar Azam, the team's talisman, was ruled out of this series opener with a hand injury, handing the captaincy to all-rounder **Salman Ali Agha** — himself no stranger to controversy, having previously picked up ICC demerit points for on-field conduct. This tour of England, running from **August 19 to September 13**, was seen as a chance for Pakistan to prove their overseas game had improved after a rocky year that included a heavy ODI series defeat in Bangladesh.
depth.why_it_matters: This isn't just one bad session — it's the latest data point in a recurring pattern that raises real questions about Pakistan's technical and mental preparation for testing overseas conditions, and it puts real pressure on a stand-in captain leading his side for the first time in a high-stakes series.
depth.ripple_effects: A poor result here could intensify scrutiny on Pakistan's team management and selection panel ahead of a long tour (three Tests, running to mid-September), and adds pressure on Babar Azam's own position once he's fit to return — does the team go back to him, or does a strong showing from Agha change that calculus?
depth.why_now: Day one of this Test only concluded within the last day, and the scale of the collapse — from a solid position to all out for 171 — is exactly the kind of fresh, dramatic swing that's generating immediate reaction and scrutiny.
depth.watch_next: How Pakistan's bowlers respond on day two to claw the match back, and whether Salman Agha's captaincy draws public comment from PCB officials or former players over the rest of the series.

key_terms.definition: A player who leads the team temporarily because the regular captain is unavailable, often through injury.

cards.title: Jordan Cox's Test chance against Pakistan is a full-circle moment born from a career-altering injury
cards.what_happened: With Jacob Bethell now injured and unavailable, Jordan Cox has been promoted to bat at number three for England's first Test against Pakistan at Headingley — the very role once denied to him by injury, now his because of someone else's. Cox has spoken this week about drawing on advice from Virat Kohli, his former captain at Royal Challengers Bengaluru, who told him to focus on enjoying the occasion rather than being weighed down by its importance. Cox described the moment as bringing a sense of **"clarity"** to his game, even as it puts him in an unfamiliar top-order role for England, two years after the injury that first cost him this exact opportunity.
key_points: **Jordan Cox** is batting at number three for England's first Test against Pakistan, filling in for the injured **Jacob Bethell**.
It's a **full-circle moment**: Bethell's own Test debut two years ago only happened because Cox broke his thumb in the nets days before his scheduled debut.
Cox credits advice from **Virat Kohli**, his former Royal Challengers Bengaluru captain, for helping him handle the pressure of Test selection.
Kohli reportedly told Cox to **enjoy the occasion** rather than let its significance overwhelm him.
Cox finally made his delayed Test debut at **The Oval in June**, batting at number seven as cover for a suspended Ben Stokes.
cards.moot: Opportunity in competitive sport is rarely fair in the moment, but setbacks and openings often connect in ways that only make sense years later — the same injury that costs you a chance can, indirectly, be what eventually creates a new one.

depth.background: Jordan Cox was on the verge of a Test debut against New Zealand two years ago, only to fracture his thumb in the nets just days before the match — forcing him to call his own father and tell him not to fly out to watch. **Jacob Bethell** stepped into the vacated spot instead, and went on to build his own England Test career from that opportunity. Cox finally got his own Test debut this June, at The Oval, playing at number seven as cover while Ben Stokes served a suspension. He also spent time playing IPL cricket for **Royal Challengers Bengaluru**, where he crossed paths with Virat Kohli, one of the format's most storied players, who has become an unlikely mentor figure to him.
depth.why_it_matters: It's a rare, clean story of professional sport's cruelty and fairness running in parallel — the same injury that once took an opportunity from Cox is, years later, the reason he's finally getting a real crack at establishing himself in England's top order.
depth.ripple_effects: A strong showing at number three could cement Cox's place in England's middle order well beyond this series, reshaping the pecking order among England's next generation of batters once Bethell returns from injury.
depth.why_now: This is directly tied to the ongoing first Test against Pakistan this week, with Cox only handed the number three role because of Bethell's current injury absence.
depth.watch_next: How Cox performs in this innings and across the series at number three, and whether it changes England's thinking on their top-order pecking order once Bethell is fit again.

key_terms.definition: One of the most demanding roles in a cricket batting order — often facing the ball early with the new ball still moving, requiring both technique and temperament.

cards.title: BCCI president Mithun Manhas faces police probe over alleged date-of-birth fabrication
cards.what_happened: A **Special Railway Magistrate's Court in Jammu** directed police at Nowabad police station to open a **preliminary inquiry** into a complaint against **BCCI president Mithun Manhas**, alleging he recorded different dates of birth at different points in his cricketing career. The complaint says Manhas's school records — from Maharaja Hari Singh Agriculture Collegiate School in Nagbani, Jammu — list his birth date as **December 9, 1977**, while the **Delhi & District Cricket Association's** official records list **October 12, 1979**, a gap of roughly two years. The complainant, **Sudershan Mehta**, has a history of conflict with Manhas, including a separate pending criminal defamation case against him. The court has asked police to submit their inquiry report by **September 3, 2026**. The underlying age-fabrication allegation remains an unproven complaint, not an established fact.
key_points: A Jammu court ordered police to investigate a complaint that **BCCI president Mithun Manhas** used **two different birth dates** at different points in his career.
His school records reportedly list his birth date as **December 9, 1977**; the Delhi & District Cricket Association's site lists **October 12, 1979** — a **two-year gap**.
The complaint was filed by **Sudershan Mehta**, a former J&K Cricket Association official and longtime Manhas critic, who also has a separate defamation case pending against Manhas.
Police must report back to the court by **September 3, 2026**.
cards.moot: Old, unresolved local disputes can resurface years later and reach all the way to the top of an organization — a junior-level grievance from a state cricket association is now a police matter involving the president of the world's richest cricket board.

depth.background: **Age fraud** — young cricketers or their guardians misstating birth dates to stay eligible for junior age-group tournaments — has been a persistent, sensitive issue in Indian domestic cricket for years. **Mithun Manhas** is a former India domestic cricketer who now serves as **president of the BCCI**, the Board of Control for Cricket in India — the world's richest and most powerful cricket board. The complainant, **Sudershan Mehta**, is a former Joint Honorary Secretary of the **Jammu & Kashmir Cricket Association** and has a long-running rivalry with Manhas, including a separate criminal defamation case he has filed against Manhas and JKCA officials.
depth.why_it_matters: This puts the sitting president of the world's richest and most powerful cricket board under an active police inquiry into his own identity documents — a serious governance headline for the BCCI regardless of the outcome. If substantiated, it would reopen long-standing questions about age-fudging in Indian domestic cricket's talent pipeline, where junior-age eligibility can shape a player's entire career path.
depth.ripple_effects: A drawn-out probe could become a distraction for the BCCI at a time it's managing India's international schedule, IPL auctions, and multiple selection controversies. It also hands ammunition to Manhas's long-standing critics within Jammu & Kashmir cricket politics, where this dispute has deep roots.
depth.why_now: The court's order directing a police inquiry was reported on August 19, 2026, reviving a years-old rivalry between Manhas and Mehta.
depth.watch_next: Watch for the police inquiry report due to the Jammu court by September 3, 2026.

key_terms.definition: Misstating a young player's birth date to keep them eligible for junior/age-restricted tournaments, a long-standing integrity issue in Indian domestic cricket.

cards.title: Hardik Pandya reportedly closing in on a KKR move — with the captaincy attached
cards.what_happened: Fresh reporting says Pandya is now believed to be closing in on a switch to **Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR)** ahead of IPL 2027, with some insider accounts suggesting he could be installed as KKR's captain — a notable escalation from earlier reports that only described "interest" or "talks." KKR has been described as the frontrunner among as many as seven interested franchises, ahead of Chennai Super Kings, which had reportedly offered players plus cash. Mumbai Indians have not confirmed any deal, maintaining their position that no trade decisions will be made until their internal season review concludes. Adding complexity: Pandya has previously been reported as unwilling to join KKR unless the franchise parts ways with coach **Abhishek Nayar**, over friction that reportedly traces back to Pandya's earlier fallout with Rohit Sharma.
key_points: Pandya is reportedly **closing in on a move to KKR**, with insiders suggesting he could be named **KKR's captain**.
**Seven IPL franchises** have been circling the India all-rounder, with **KKR and CSK** the two frontrunners.
**Mumbai Indians** — Pandya's current team and the side he currently captains — have not confirmed any deal and say their season review is still ongoing.
A KKR move would reunite Pandya with the club that gave him his IPL start, but tension reportedly persists over **KKR coach Abhishek Nayar**, whom Pandya has clashed with before.
No trade has been officially completed — this remains insider reporting, not a confirmed deal.
cards.moot: In sports trade sagas, watch for the specificity of claims escalating (from "talks" to "captaincy") as a signal that a deal is getting closer — vague interest and a concrete role attached are very different stages of negotiation.

thread.previously: We reported Mumbai Indians pushed back on claims that trade talks over Hardik Pandya were underway, insisting nothing would move until their post-season review finished.
thread.changed: New reporting says Pandya is now believed to be closing in on a move to Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR) for IPL 2027 — with insiders suggesting he could take over as KKR's captain, a significantly bigger claim than the earlier "talks are underway" reports.

depth.background: Hardik Pandya is one of Indian cricket's most valuable all-rounders and currently captains Mumbai Indians (MI) in the IPL, having returned to the franchise in a high-profile trade back in 2024. Every IPL offseason now includes a formal trade and auction window where franchises can move contracted players, and speculation about star players moving is a fixture of the build-up to each new season — MI have previously and repeatedly denied that talks over Pandya were serious, even as reports of interest from multiple franchises kept building.
depth.why_it_matters: If confirmed, this would be one of the biggest IPL trades in years — moving a marquee all-rounder and giving him the captaincy of a different franchise, reshaping both MI's and KKR's squads and leadership heading into 2027.
depth.ripple_effects: A Pandya-to-KKR move would force Mumbai Indians to find a new captain and rebuild their all-rounder options, while KKR would need to resolve the coaching-staff tension reportedly standing in the way before any deal can close. It also keeps the IPL trade window as the dominant off-field storyline heading into the 2027 auction cycle.
depth.why_now: This is a live, developing trade saga in the run-up to the IPL 2027 mega-auction window, and today's reports mark the first time the captaincy angle — not just a playing move — has surfaced.
depth.watch_next: Whether Mumbai Indians' season review concludes with an official confirmation or denial of a Pandya trade, and whether the Nayar coaching-staff issue at KKR gets resolved one way or the other.

prev_ref.title: BCCI's selectors are furious at the board's own secretary over a Rohit Sharma retirement denial

cards.title: Rohit Sharma is picked for the West Indies ODIs, but the selectors who wanted him gone still feel burned
cards.what_happened: India's chosen squad for the upcoming **West Indies ODI series** confirms Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli both remain in the fold for the 50-over format, resolving — for now — the retirement speculation that had built up. But the underlying tension hasn't resolved: selectors are reportedly still upset that BCCI secretary **Devajit Saikia** publicly reaffirmed Rohit's place in the team's plans just before the squad announcement, which they saw as reversing an internal lean toward transitioning away from him, seemingly in reaction to public and social-media pressure. That friction is reportedly now bleeding into a separate decision: chief selector **Ajit Agarkar** completes three years in the role this September and is eligible for a one-year extension, with BCCI office-bearers expected to take up that decision once the ongoing Sri Lanka Test series ends — with Rohit's ODI future said to be one of the sticking points behind the scenes.
key_points: **Rohit Sharma**, 38, has been retained in India's ODI squad for the **West Indies series**, alongside **Virat Kohli**, 36 — both now play only the 50-over format.
Selectors reportedly feel **"betrayed"** that BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia publicly backed Rohit after internal discussions had leaned toward moving past him for the **2027 World Cup**.
Shubman Gill, 25, has separately been named India's new **ODI captain**, taking over the role from Rohit.
The rift is now tangled up with chief selector **Ajit Agarkar's** own future — his three-year term ends in September and BCCI is due to discuss his extension.
Selectors believe the board's public stance shifted **in response to social-media backlash**, not fresh cricketing judgment.
cards.moot: In big sporting organizations, personnel disputes are rarely just about one player — they're often proxy fights over who holds real decision-making power, and the player is just where that fight becomes visible.

thread.previously: We reported that BCCI selectors were furious after board secretary Devajit Saikia publicly denied Rohit Sharma was being pushed toward retirement — a denial selectors felt was made under social-media pressure and contradicted the board's own internal direction.
thread.changed: Today's reporting confirms the practical outcome: Rohit Sharma has in fact been kept in India's squad for the West Indies ODIs alongside Virat Kohli, both playing ODI-only roles. The friction hasn't gone away — it's now reportedly spilling into chief selector Ajit Agarkar's own position, with BCCI office-bearers expected to discuss his one-year extension, due in September, against the backdrop of this same disagreement.

depth.background: India's chief selector picks the national squads, but the **BCCI (Board of Control for Cricket in India)** — the sport's governing body — sits above the selection committee and can shape or override its direction through its office-bearers. Rohit Sharma has already retired from **Test and T20I cricket**, leaving ODIs as his last format, and with the **2027 ODI World Cup** on the horizon, selectors have been debating whether a 38-year-old should still be central to that plan. Shubman Gill's rise — already India's Test captain — into the ODI captaincy as well signals the succession is already underway even as Rohit keeps playing.
depth.why_it_matters: This is a governance story as much as a cricket one: it shows India's chief selectors can be publicly overruled by the board's administrative leadership, which raises questions about who actually controls team selection heading into a home-soil-adjacent World Cup cycle.
depth.ripple_effects: If Agarkar isn't extended, or leaves under a cloud, India heads toward the 2027 World Cup with a reshuffled selection committee at a sensitive moment in the Rohit-to-Gill transition. It also sets a precedent other senior players and their camps will note — that public and social pressure can shape BCCI's official line on team selection.
depth.why_now: The West Indies squad announcement forced BCCI's hand on Rohit's immediate status, while Agarkar's September deadline means the deeper power struggle over who controls selection is coming to a head at almost the same time.
depth.watch_next: Whether Ajit Agarkar gets his one-year extension as chief selector when BCCI office-bearers meet after the Sri Lanka Test series concludes.

cards.title: A DRS scare and alarm bells: inside Australia's reckoning after its historic loss to Bangladesh
cards.what_happened: In the first Test in Darwin, Bangladesh dominated a full-strength Australian side across all four days, winning by nine wickets to record one of the most one-sided Test wins away from home in the sport's recent history. Australia had gone into the match having won 11 of its previous 13 Tests and sitting top of the World Test Championship standings, making the defeat land as a genuine shock rather than a minor upset. On Day 1, Steve Smith was given not out on a caught-behind review off Ebadot Hossain that looked close on the stump-mic audio; Smith later admitted in a post-match interview that he believed he had actually edged it, joking 'technology saved me today.' Australian newspapers have since run scathing post-mortems on the batting collapse and team culture, and the second and final Test of the series begins August 22 in Mackay, Queensland, with Australia's established stars now under real pressure to respond.
key_points: Australia lost to Bangladesh by **nine wickets** in Darwin — one of the most humiliating defeats in Australian Test history
A full-strength Australian side that had **won 11 of its last 13 Tests** and topped the World Test Championship table was outplayed in every department
Star batter **Steve Smith** survived a contentious caught-behind review on Day 1, later admitting **'I think so, yeah'** when asked if he had actually nicked it
Bangladesh, ranked **ninth in the world**, had managed just **one win in 26 previous SENA-country Tests** and hadn't played a Test in Australia for **23 years**
Australian media has torn into the result, with the second and final Test starting **August 22 in Mackay** now billed as a must-win response
cards.moot: In cricket, a strong recent record and a stacked lineup are not a guarantee against an upset — form and rankings describe the past, not what happens over four days against a team playing above itself.

depth.background: Australia entered this series against Bangladesh as overwhelming favorites — a settled, in-form Test team against a side that had almost no history of winning in seam-friendly conditions overseas (the 'SENA' countries: South Africa, England, New Zealand, Australia). Test cricket's Decision Review System (DRS) uses replays, ball-tracking, and stump-microphone audio to help umpires check close calls like edges behind the wicket; a 'not out' review that looks close on the audio, as happened with Smith, often reignites cricket's long-running 'Spirit of Cricket' debate about players walking versus relying on technology.
depth.why_it_matters: This is being treated in Australia as a genuine crisis moment for a team that had looked untouchable — a warning that a stacked lineup and a strong recent record can still be blown apart by a lower-ranked side on the right day, and that even senior players like Smith are not immune to close-call controversy.
depth.ripple_effects: Expect Australian selectors to face pressure over batting-order changes ahead of Mackay, renewed debate about DRS reliability and player honesty around edges, and a confidence boost for Bangladesh cricket heading into future overseas tours.
depth.why_now: The fallout and 'Spirit of Cricket' debate have continued to build in Australian media in the days since the Darwin Test ended, with the series decider now just days away.
depth.watch_next: Whether Australia makes personnel changes for the Mackay Test, and whether Bangladesh can back up the Darwin result to win the series outright.

key_terms.definition: A technology-assisted system using replays, ball-tracking, and stump microphones that lets players challenge an umpire's on-field decision.

cards.title: Manav Suthar's 10-wicket haul seals India's 165-run win over Sri Lanka — and quiets the noise around Gill's captaincy
cards.what_happened: India completed a 165-run victory over Sri Lanka on the fifth and final day in Galle, bowling the hosts out for 206 in their second innings. Left-arm spinner Manav Suthar, playing just his second Test, took 6 for 55 to finish with a 10-wicket match haul, turning the game with a triple-wicket maiden in the 76th over that broke a key partnership, bowled Jayasuriya for a golden duck, and had Kumara caught behind. The win — built on Padikkal's first-innings 167 and contributions from Rishabh Pant — gave India a 1-0 lead in the two-match series and was India's 600th Test match overall. Captain Shubman Gill, who had faced criticism over his captaincy, called the win "very satisfying," explaining the team wasn't sure the match would even finish given the weather and had targeted around 400 in the third innings before pushing for the result.
key_points: India beat Sri Lanka by **165 runs** in Galle, taking a **1-0 lead** in the two-Test series.
Spinner **Manav Suthar**, playing only his **second Test**, took a **10-wicket match haul** (6-55 in the second innings).
Sri Lanka were bowled out for **206**, with Suthar breaking the game open via a **triple-wicket maiden** in the 76th over.
It was India's landmark **600th Test match** — and a statement win for captain **Shubman Gill**, whose leadership had been under scrutiny.
Gill credited the bowlers and a tricky pitch, saying the team "**responded well**" despite uncertainty over whether the match would even finish.
cards.moot: A captain's reputation often rides on results as much as on decisions — the same tactics that look risky in a loss get called 'clinical' the moment the team wins.

thread.previously: Yesterday, India had bowled Sri Lanka out for 284 to take a 178-run first-innings lead, a position of strength that had temporarily quieted criticism of Gill's captaincy.
thread.changed: India completed the win today — by 165 runs — with Manav Suthar's 10-wicket match haul sealing it, turning Gill's 'for now' reprieve into a clear, result-backed vindication.

depth.background: Shubman Gill took over India's Test captaincy in a transition year and has faced persistent public scrutiny over his tactical decisions and results, with critics questioning whether the team's newer, younger core could deliver away from home. Devdutt Padikkal's first-innings 167 had already set up a commanding 178-run lead by the fourth day, but Test matches can swing quickly on turning subcontinent pitches, and Sri Lanka's second-innings fightback kept the result in doubt into the final day.
depth.why_it_matters: A dominant, spin-driven win on the road quiets — at least for now — the criticism Gill had been facing as a young captain, and gives India momentum with one Test still to play in the series.
depth.ripple_effects: A standout Suthar performance in only his second Test strengthens India's spin-bowling depth heading into future subcontinent tours; a winning captain also reduces pressure on selectors ahead of India's next assignments.
depth.why_now: The match concluded today on its scheduled final day, with the result only becoming certain once Sri Lanka's second innings collapsed.
depth.watch_next: The second and final Test of the series, where Sri Lanka will need to win to level the series.

key_terms.definition: An over (six balls) in which the batting side scores no runs — a 'triple-wicket maiden' means three wickets fell in that same over.

cards.title: BCCI's selectors are furious at the board's own secretary over a Rohit Sharma retirement denial
cards.what_happened: According to multiple reports this week, India's selection committee had privately told Rohit Sharma they intended to move on from him in ODIs once the England series concluded. BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia then went public saying there had been no such discussion and that Rohit would continue as a regular member of the side for as long as he remained part of India's plans — a statement selectors are said to have found frustrating, since it publicly contradicted their own call without consulting them first. That tension now feeds into a separate, higher-stakes conversation: Agarkar's own three-year term as chairman of selectors runs out in September, and under the current rules he's eligible for a one-year extension. The BCCI is reportedly keen to keep him in the role through the 2027 World Cup given his record — two ICC titles during his tenure — but a formal decision is expected only after the board meets him directly, with some reports floating VVS Laxman as an alternative if talks don't go smoothly.
key_points: Selectors had reportedly told **Rohit Sharma** they planned to move on from him after the England ODI series.
BCCI secretary **Devajit Saikia** then publicly said Rohit remains a **'regular member'** of the ODI team, contradicting that plan.
The selection committee, led by **Ajit Agarkar**, is said to be unhappy the board undercut their call in public.
Agarkar's own three-year term as chief selector **expires in September**, and the BCCI is set to meet him about an extension.
Reports suggest the board wants Agarkar to stay through the **2027 ODI World Cup**, but the rift adds uncertainty.
cards.moot: In any organization, public statements from leadership that contradict what a team's own decision-makers privately agreed on tend to create friction — because it signals whose word actually carries authority.

depth.background: India's chief selector, a role currently held by former fast bowler **Ajit Agarkar** since 2023, leads the panel that picks the national team and is meant to make those calls independent of the board's day-to-day management. Rohit Sharma, India's ODI captain for years, has already retired from Tests, and speculation about his ODI future has followed him through this year as India builds toward the 2027 ODI World Cup. In July, after Rohit played a match-winning innings at Lord's, Saikia had publicly waved off retirement talk — but the selectors' actual internal plan, according to these new reports, was reportedly the opposite.
depth.why_it_matters: This isn't really about one player's future — it's a rare public glimpse of the BCCI's secretariat (administrators) overruling or embarrassing its own cricket selectors, which raises the question of who actually controls team selection in Indian cricket: the selectors, or the board's administration.
depth.ripple_effects: If Agarkar leaves or the rift deepens, it could reshape the selection committee heading into the 2027 World Cup cycle, affecting not just Rohit's fate but the broader transition of India's ODI core. It also puts Rohit in an awkward public spot, forced to play out his career amid conflicting signals about whether the team wants him.
depth.why_now: The tension surfaced because Agarkar's contract decision is due before September, forcing the board and selectors to have the conversation about the team's direction — and Rohit's role in it — right now rather than later.
depth.watch_next: The outcome of the BCCI's meeting with Agarkar on his tenure, and whether Rohit's ODI selection status is clarified one way or the other before India's next series.

key_terms.definition: The head of the panel that picks India's national cricket squads — a role meant to be independent of the board's administrative staff.

cards.title: Hardik Pandya reportedly won't join KKR unless the franchise drops coach Abhishek Nayar — a grudge that traces back to Rohit Sharma

cards.moot: Personal relationships and old grudges inside a dressing room can carry as much weight as money or performance when it comes to deciding a major trade — professional sport is still run by people with memories.

depth.why_now: IPL franchises are actively working the trade and retention window ahead of the 2027 mega-auction cycle, and Pandya's future has become the marquee storyline of this period.

cards.title: Moeen Ali quietly reversed his retirement from English domestic cricket after his overseas T20 gamble ran into trouble
cards.what_happened: Moeen Ali initially retired from **English domestic cricket** specifically to secure NOCs for the **Global Super League** and the **Caribbean Premier League**, prioritizing the overseas T20 paycheck route. He has since **reversed that decision**, signing with **Yorkshire** ahead of this year's **T20 Blast** and registering for **The Hundred** draft with a base price of **£75,000** — putting him back in the domestic English pipeline he'd stepped away from. The move comes alongside other veteran comebacks in the same window: **James Anderson**, who retired from international cricket, has also entered The Hundred draft in an attempt to revive his playing career, having not played competitively since July.
key_points: Moeen had **retired from English domestic cricket** to free himself up for the **Global Super League** and **Caribbean Premier League**, chasing lucrative overseas T20 deals.
He has now **reversed that decision** and signed for **Yorkshire** ahead of the T20 Blast.
He's also **registered for The Hundred draft** at a base price of **£75,000**.
The saga shows the tension between chasing **overseas T20 leagues** and staying eligible for **domestic county deals** back home.
It comes as **James Anderson** has also entered The Hundred draft, aiming to revive his playing career after international retirement.
cards.moot: Chasing the biggest available payday isn't always the optimal career move — giving up steady, established opportunities for a bigger but less certain one can backfire, and the smartest players build in a way back if it does.

depth.background: English all-rounder **Moeen Ali** originally stepped away from domestic English cricket so he could obtain **No-Objection Certificates (NOCs)** — official clearance the ECB requires before an English player can sign for lucrative overseas T20 leagues like the Caribbean Premier League or the Global Super League, since playing at home and abroad at the same time can create scheduling and release conflicts. Giving up domestic status was meant to simplify that path, but it also meant losing his place in England's T20 Blast and Hundred pipeline.
depth.why_it_matters: This is a rare public U-turn that exposes the real financial and scheduling tug-of-war modern freelance T20 cricketers face — chasing the biggest overseas paydays can mean sacrificing the domestic deals and visibility that sustain a career longer-term.
depth.ripple_effects: Yorkshire and The Hundred benefit from a recognizable, experienced player returning to the pool right as the draft approaches, while it signals to other English freelancers that reversing an overseas-focused retirement is a viable, low-stigma option if the numbers don't work out as planned.
depth.why_now: The reversal lands just ahead of The Hundred draft and the T20 Blast season, the exact windows where his domestic eligibility status matters most.
depth.watch_next: Whether Moeen gets picked up in The Hundred draft and how he performs after this back-and-forth in his schedule and commitments.

key_terms.definition: Official permission a national cricket board must give a player before they can sign with a foreign T20 league, used to manage scheduling conflicts with home commitments.

cards.title: Joe Root scraps England's midnight curfew for the Pakistan Tests, and Nasser Hussain calls it 'a grown-up decision'
cards.what_happened: Root abolished the team's midnight curfew as his first act back as captain, telling players to behave like **'grown adults'** instead of policing them with a fixed rule. Former England captain **Nasser Hussain** endorsed the move on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, calling it **'just a grown-up decision'** and arguing that if players don't act responsibly, the right response is to **fine them first, and drop them if it continues** — rather than impose blanket restrictions on the whole squad. Hussain added that needing a curfew in the first place 'shows how bad a place they were in.' The change comes as Root leads England into the opening Test of a three-match series against Pakistan at Headingley, his first Test in charge since 2022.
key_points: Root scrapped the **midnight curfew** in his **first act since returning as England Test captain**.
The curfew was brought in after **Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson broke it**, missing a Test after a nightclub incident.
Former captain **Nasser Hussain** backed the call, saying **'a professional sporting outfit shouldn't need a curfew.'**
Root wants players treated as **'grown adults'**, with fines and then being dropped as the real deterrent instead of blanket rules.
cards.moot: Rules brought in during a crisis often outlive the crisis itself — sometimes leadership means removing a restriction and replacing it with real accountability, rather than adding more rules on top of the ones that already didn't work.

depth.background: England's Test team introduced player-behaviour guidelines, including a midnight curfew, after a string of off-field alcohol-related incidents during the **'Bazball' era**. The rule became a flashpoint when then-captain **Ben Stokes and bowler Gus Atkinson** were left out of a Test against New Zealand after being caught breaking it following a nightclub visit. **Joe Root** has now returned to the England Test captaincy for a second stint — having previously stepped down in 2022 — and this Pakistan series, starting today at Headingley, is his first assignment back in charge.
depth.why_it_matters: This is a real test of Root's leadership philosophy at the start of his second captaincy stint: trusting players over policing them. If it goes wrong, the accountability now sits squarely with Root rather than a rulebook.
depth.ripple_effects: It sets the tone for England's dressing-room culture heading into a big season, and other captains and boards — English or otherwise — will be watching whether a trust-based approach holds up better than the rules it replaces. Any future off-field incident during this series will now be judged against Root's personal call to remove the curfew.
depth.why_now: The decision was made as Root's first act on returning to the captaincy, timed to take effect right as the Pakistan series — his first Test in charge since 2022 — gets underway today at Headingley.
depth.watch_next: Whether England's discipline holds up through the three-Test series against Pakistan, and whether results validate Root's 'trust the players' approach.

cards.title: Babar Azam ruled out of the Headingley Test with a hand injury — Salman Ali Agha steps in as Pakistan captain
cards.what_happened: Pakistan confirmed that **Babar Azam will not play the first Test** against England at Headingley after failing to recover from a right-hand injury. Babar was originally hit on the hand during Pakistan's Test series in the **West Indies** earlier this month, then took a further blow to the same hand from an **England Under-19 seamer** during a tour warm-up match at Beckenham. Head coach **Sarfaraz Ahmed** confirmed there is no fracture in the finger, but that Babar could not be cleared to play despite working through a brief net session. In his absence, **vice-captain Salman Ali Agha** will lead Pakistan for the opening Test, which began today. Pakistan's management indicated Babar's absence is for now confined to just this first Test of the three-match series.

**Salman Ali Agha** will captain Pakistan in Babar's place for the opening Test.
Babar was struck on the **same hand twice** — first against West Indies, then again in a **warm-up match at Beckenham** against an England Under-19 seamer.

The injury comes just as **Joe Root** returns to the England captaincy for the first time since **2022**, making this a first Test both sides expected their comeback captains to lead.
cards.moot: In team sports, an injury to one key figure right before a big event doesn't just remove a player — it can reshape the entire leadership dynamic and pressure distribution of the whole team overnight.

thread.previously: As of yesterday, both Joe Root and Babar Azam were set to lead their sides in comeback roles at Headingley — Root returning to the England captaincy for the first time since giving it up in 2022, and Babar back in charge of a Pakistan side searching for direction.

depth.background: Both England and Pakistan arrive at this three-Test series with captains making comebacks. Joe Root, one of England's greatest batters, gave up the England captaincy in 2022 after a difficult run and is now returning to lead the side for the first time since. Babar Azam, Pakistan's Test captain, has also been trying to steady a team that has struggled for consistency, arriving at Headingley on the back of Pakistan's first away Test win in three years. depth.why_it_matters: This was billed as a clash between two comeback captains — Root's return for England, Babar's for Pakistan — and now half of that storyline is gone before a ball was bowled in anger, forcing a largely untested Salman Ali Agha into a high-pressure leadership role in his first major Test as captain.
depth.ripple_effects: A stand-in captain leading a touring side in a marquee series adds pressure on Pakistan's dressing room at a time it's already trying to build momentum after ending a three-year away-Test win drought. depth.watch_next: Watch whether Babar recovers in time to return for the second or third Test of the series, and how Salman Ali Agha performs in his place as captain.

cards.title: Two cricket teams in crisis, two comeback captains: Root and Babar collide today at Headingley
cards.what_happened: England and Pakistan begin a three-Test series today at **Headingley** in Leeds, with the first ball scheduled for **11:00am local time**. Joe Root captains England for the first time since relinquishing the role in 2022, while Babar Azam leads Pakistan back into a series after being restored as Test captain. Pakistan's build-up was clouded by uncertainty over Babar's fitness after he was struck on the right hand during a warm-up match in Kent, though he has been cleared to play. Both sides come in out of form — Pakistan sit eighth in the World Test Championship table with just two wins in six matches, while England, seventh, are coming off a 2-1 home series defeat to New Zealand.
key_points: **Joe Root** returns as England's full-time Test captain today, having given up the role back in **2022**.
**Babar Azam** leads Pakistan again after being reinstated, following a difficult run under predecessor **Shan Masood**.
Pakistan enter with an injury scare — Babar was **struck on the hand** during a Kent practice match before the series.
Both teams arrive under pressure: **England seventh, Pakistan eighth** in the current World Test Championship standings.
England open a new coaching era too, ending the **Bazball** period defined by Ben Stokes and Brendon McCullum.

depth.background: England's Test team spent the last several years under captain **Ben Stokes** and coach **Brendon McCullum**, playing an aggressive style nicknamed 'Bazball' that transformed the team's results and reputation. Stokes has since stepped back from Test captaincy, McCullum has moved to focus on England's white-ball teams, and Root — England's most experienced modern batter, who first captained the side from 2017 to 2022 — has taken the job back. Pakistan, meanwhile, have churned through captains, with **Babar Azam** now reinstated after Shan Masood's tenure produced a poor run of results, including 14 losses in their last 18 Tests.

cards.title: England hands its Test team to a foreign coach for the first time in the Bazball era — and it's not who Ben Stokes wanted
cards.what_happened: The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) has named **Stephen Fleming** as its new men's Test head coach on a four-year contract through September 2030, marking his first job coaching at international level despite a long, successful franchise-cricket coaching career. He replaces Brendon McCullum in the Test role specifically — McCullum remains in charge of England's white-ball teams — and arrives as Joe Root simultaneously takes back the Test captaincy he gave up in 2022. Fleming does have prior ties to English cricket, having previously played for Middlesex, Yorkshire, and Nottinghamshire (captaining Notts to a county title in 2005) and coached Southern Brave in The Hundred.
key_points: **Stephen Fleming**, the former New Zealand captain and longtime Chennai Super Kings coach, is England's new men's Test head coach.
He signed a **four-year deal** with the ECB running through **September 2030** — his first-ever international coaching job.
He replaces **Brendon McCullum**, who stepped down from the Test role after England's series loss to New Zealand in June but stays on to run England's white-ball teams.
The appointment comes as **Joe Root** simultaneously returns as full-time Test captain.
It's a pointed twist: former captain **Ben Stokes** recently said he'd like the England head coach job **one day** — it just went to someone else, now.

depth.background: England's Test side has been coached by fellow New Zealander Brendon McCullum since 2022, alongside captain Ben Stokes, in a partnership that produced the aggressive 'Bazball' era and transformed the team's results and public profile. That era effectively ended when Stokes stepped back from the Test captaincy and McCullum, after a home series defeat to New Zealand in June, chose to step down from the Test coaching role specifically while remaining in charge of England's white-ball (ODI and T20) sides. **Stephen Fleming** built his post-playing reputation primarily in franchise cricket, most notably as the long-serving head coach of the Chennai Super Kings in the IPL, rather than in international coaching.

cards.title: Rishabh Pant returns to Delhi Capitals in a blockbuster swap that sends Kuldeep Yadav to Lucknow
cards.what_happened: Delhi Capitals and Lucknow Super Giants **officially completed a trade** ahead of IPL 2027: **Rishabh Pant returns to Delhi Capitals**, the team he represented for nine seasons and 111 matches (2016-2024, the most appearances by any player in DC's history), while **Kuldeep Yadav moves to Lucknow Super Giants** after five seasons and 72 wickets in 65 matches for Delhi. On the financial side, Pant rejoins DC at a **revised fee of ₹15 crore**, down sharply from the **₹27 crore** LSG paid to sign him in the 2025 mega auction. Kuldeep moves at his **existing ₹13.5 crore fee**. The fee gap means **LSG gains roughly ₹13.5 crore** in extra purse space for the next auction, while **DC's purse is reduced by ₹1.5 crore**.
key_points: **Rishabh Pant** is heading back to **Delhi Capitals**, the franchise he played nine seasons for, in a trade with Lucknow Super Giants.
**Kuldeep Yadav** moves the other way to **Lucknow Super Giants**, after five seasons taking 72 wickets for Delhi.
Pant rejoins DC at a **cut fee of ₹15 crore**, down from the **₹27 crore** LSG paid for him in the 2025 mega auction — roughly a **44% pay cut**.
Kuldeep moves at his existing **₹13.5 crore** fee, leaving LSG with **~₹13.5 crore extra** in their purse for the next auction, while DC loses ₹1.5 crore from theirs.
Pant made **111 appearances for Delhi** from 2016-2024, the most of any player in the franchise's history.

depth.background: The IPL (Indian Premier League) allows franchises to **trade contracted players** between seasons, subject to negotiated fees that adjust each team's remaining auction budget ('purse'). Rishabh Pant, one of India's most recognizable wicketkeeper-batters, spent nearly a decade as the face of Delhi Capitals before a big-money move to Lucknow Super Giants in the 2025 mega auction. Kuldeep Yadav, a left-arm wrist-spin bowler, had been one of Delhi's most effective bowlers over five seasons. This trade effectively **reunites Pant with his old franchise** while Delhi gives up a key bowler to make it happen.

cards.title: Keith Barker retires at 39 after a knee injury cuts short his comeback season at Warwickshire
cards.what_happened: Keith Barker has announced his retirement from professional cricket after a **17-season career**, ending a comeback stint at **Warwickshire** — the county where he made his name — that was cut short by a persistent **knee complaint**. Across ten seasons at Edgbaston (2009-2018) he took **357 wickets** and scored **six first-class centuries**, and was part of the side that won the **2012 County Championship**. After moving to Hampshire for the 2019 season, he added a further **191 wickets and 1,975 runs**, cementing his reputation as one of county cricket's most dependable all-rounders.
key_points: Left-arm all-rounder **Keith Barker** has retired from professional cricket after a **17-season career**.
He returned to **Warwickshire** this summer at age 39 hoping for one more good year.
A persistent **knee complaint** forced the decision, cutting the comeback short.
At Edgbaston alone (2009-2018) he took **357 wickets** and scored **six centuries**, helping win the **2012 County Championship**.
At Hampshire (from 2019) he added **191 more wickets** and nearly **2,000 runs**.

depth.background: **Keith Barker** spent a decade at **Warwickshire** (2009-2018), becoming one of the county's most reliable all-rounders and helping the club win the **County Championship title in 2012**. He then moved to **Hampshire** ahead of the 2019 season, continuing to perform as a genuine batting-and-bowling all-rounder. This year, at 39, he rejoined Warwickshire on a short-term deal for one more season.

cards.title: BCCI expands anti-corruption monitoring to every state T20 league after a TNPL player smuggled in an undeclared phone
cards.what_happened: The BCCI announced it is expanding **ACSU anti-corruption monitoring to cover every match in every state-run T20 league**, a first for the board, after detecting a rise in unauthorized approaches to players, franchise owners and team officials by suspected bookmakers. The immediate trigger was an incident in the **Tamil Nadu Premier League (TNPL)**, where a player was fined **₹1 lakh** and suspended after being caught carrying an undeclared mobile phone into the restricted players' area — a rule breach because unmonitored phones are one of the easiest ways for a player to be contacted or to pass on information during a match. BCCI secretary **Devajit Saikia** publicly backed a zero-tolerance approach, saying even a relatively minor breach like undeclared phone possession would now draw firm action, framing it as part of a broader effort to close gaps bookmakers could exploit across the many state leagues that have sprung up in recent years.
key_points: BCCI's **Anti-Corruption and Security Unit (ACSU)** will now cover **every match** in state-run T20 leagues, not just marquee tournaments
The trigger: a **Tamil Nadu Premier League (TNPL)** player was fined **₹1 lakh** and suspended for carrying an undeclared phone into the restricted players' area
BCCI has detected a **rise in unauthorized approaches** to players, owners and officials by suspected bookmakers across state leagues
BCCI secretary **Devajit Saikia** is publicly pushing a **zero-tolerance stance**, even for minor breaches like phone possession
State T20 leagues have multiplied across India in recent years, creating far more matches for corruption units to realistically police

depth.background: India's **state T20 leagues** — like the Tamil Nadu Premier League (TNPL), Karnataka Premier League, and similar tournaments in other states — have multiplied over the past decade as a lower-tier, franchise-style feeder circuit below the IPL, giving domestic players exposure and a bit of extra income. Because these leagues involve far more matches, smaller budgets, and less scrutiny than the IPL, they've long been seen as a softer target for match-fixing approaches by bookmakers, who typically try to recruit less-well-paid or less-experienced players. The BCCI's **Anti-Corruption and Security Unit (ACSU)** exists to police exactly this kind of risk — restricting player phone access during matches, monitoring betting patterns, and investigating approaches — but has historically concentrated its heaviest resources on the IPL rather than the many state leagues.

cards.title: ICC fines two Pakistan pacers for send-off celebrations in their World Test Championship opener
cards.what_happened: The **ICC** sanctioned Pakistan fast bowlers **Khurram Shahzad** and **Mohammad Abbas** for breaching Level 1 of its Code of Conduct during the **opening Test** of the current **World Test Championship** cycle against the **West Indies**. The charges relate to on-field celebrations, words, or gestures directed at batters after dismissing them, which match officials judged to be insulting, provocative, or likely to provoke an aggressive response. As a Level 1 breach, the sanctions are expected to be limited to reprimands and/or fines rather than any playing suspension.
key_points: Pakistan bowlers **Khurram Shahzad** and **Mohammad Abbas** were sanctioned by the **ICC**.
The breach came during the **opening Test** of the new World Test Championship cycle against the **West Indies**.
Both were found to have breached **Level 1** of the ICC's Code of Conduct.
The charge relates to on-field words or gestures toward dismissed batters judged **insulting or provocative**.
Level 1 breaches typically carry a **reprimand and/or a fine**, not a playing ban.

depth.background: Cricket's global governing body, the **ICC**, enforces a tiered Code of Conduct to police player behavior on the field. **Level 1** is the mildest tier, covering things like excessive celebrating after a wicket in a way that targets or provokes the dismissed batter — common in fast-bowling send-offs, where a bowler reacts aggressively toward a batter they've just dismissed. Punishments escalate through the levels, with the most serious breaches carrying match bans.

cards.title: Pakistan is set to drop Shaheen Afridi from Tests over workload — so he's out playing domestic cricket instead
cards.what_happened: Pakistan's selectors are reportedly set to leave **Shaheen Shah Afridi** out of the Test squads for the team's upcoming tours of the **West Indies and England**, citing the need to manage his workload across a packed international schedule. Afridi is said to be unhappy with the decision. In the meantime, rather than being rested outright, Afridi has been playing in Pakistan's domestic **National Champions Cup**, where his team, Sparco Paints Pakistan Gold, beat UOL Pakistan Whites by five wickets on **August 16** to reach the tournament final — Afridi himself took **3 wickets for 26 runs** in the match. Alongside him, fellow pacers **Naseem Shah** and **Hasan Ali**, and veteran spinner **Noman Ali**, are also reportedly being moved out of the Test line-up as part of a wider shake-up of Pakistan's red-ball attack.
key_points: Shaheen Shah Afridi is likely to be **left out of Pakistan's Test squads** for the West Indies and England tours.
The stated reason is **workload management** — but Afridi is reportedly **unhappy** about the decision.
While the squad call plays out, Afridi has been turning out in Pakistan's **National Champions Cup** domestic tournament.
His side reached the final on August 16 with Afridi taking **3 wickets for 26 runs**.
Fellow pacers **Naseem Shah** and **Hasan Ali**, plus spinner **Noman Ali**, are also reportedly being eased out of the Test set-up.

depth.background: **Shaheen Shah Afridi** is Pakistan's premier fast bowler and a former Test vice-captain, central to the team's red-ball attack for years. Cricket boards increasingly rotate and rest fast bowlers across a packed international calendar to protect them from injury and burnout, a practice known as **workload management** — but the players on the receiving end don't always agree with the timing or the selectors' reasoning, and disputes over who gets rested can become selection flashpoints.

cards.title: Jemimah Rodrigues ruled out of the Women's Asia Cup and Asian Games with a hamstring tear — Pratika Rawal steps in
cards.what_happened: Rodrigues **tore her right hamstring** — described as a 'high-grade' tear, the more serious end of the injury scale — while playing for Southern Brave in The Hundred on **August 3**. After medical assessment, India's Women's Selection Committee ruled her out of both the upcoming **Women's Asia Cup**, which runs from **August 28 to September 13** in Dubai, and the **Asian Games** later this year. **Pratika Rawal**, who has previously played Test cricket for India, has been named as her replacement, earning a recall to the white-ball squad. The rest of the squad remains largely settled around captain **Harmanpreet Kaur** and vice-captain **Smriti Mandhana**.
key_points: Rodrigues suffered a **high-grade right hamstring tear** playing for Southern Brave in **The Hundred** on August 3.
She is ruled out of both the **Women's Asia Cup (Aug 28–Sep 13)** and the **Asian Games**.
**Pratika Rawal** has been named her replacement, earning a recall to the squad.
**Harmanpreet Kaur** continues as captain with **Smriti Mandhana** as vice-captain.
It's the second major batting reshuffle in the squad, after 18-year-old **G. Kamalini** was added as second wicketkeeper.

depth.background: Jemimah Rodrigues is one of India's most important middle-order batters in white-ball cricket and had been named in India's squad for the **Women's Asia Cup 2026** in the UAE, a tournament India has dominated with seven titles historically. She'd been playing in **The Hundred**, England's short-format franchise league, for Southern Brave — a common pre-tournament tune-up for international players — when she picked up the injury.
